Automakers are also taking steps to reduce the likelihood of battery fires caused by flooding. Improved sealants and battery enclosures are being developed to limit water intrusion, and companies are working closely with researchers to create safer battery chemistries.

“These events provide valuable lessons,” says Dr. Morgan. “Manufacturers are examining battery packs for better sealing technologies and using coatings that can prevent saltwater from reaching critical components. The industry is invested in making E.V.s as resilient and safe as possible, even under extreme conditions.”

**A Rare but Manageable Concern**  
For prospective and current E.V. owners, the bottom line is that while saltwater submersion can lead to battery fires, these situations remain uncommon. With the proper precautions—such as moving your vehicle to safer ground before a storm and seeking professional help if it’s flooded—most risks can be minimized. As engineers, scientists, and firefighters continue to adapt and improve safety measures, the fear of an E.V. catching fire in the aftermath of a hurricane is likely to diminish even further.

“E.V.s represent a shift toward a cleaner, more sustainable transportation system,” says Conway. “Understanding their unique characteristics helps us be better prepared. As we learn more, we’ll keep refining our response and prevention strategies, ensuring that E.V.s are as safe as they are innovative.”

If you’ve ever worn an N95 mask, you might have wondered what its name really means. This type of mask first gained wide recognition among the general public during times of health crises, but it’s long been a standard piece of protective equipment in hospitals, construction sites, and laboratories. The good news is: the explanation is simpler than you might think.

“The ‘N95’ designation is a strict technical standard, not just a catchy name,” explains Dr. Jennifer Lee, a pulmonologist at a leading medical center. According to the U.S. National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH), masks are tested against specific criteria to ensure they’re effective filters of fine airborne particles. The “N” stands for “Not resistant to oil,” while the “95” indicates that the mask can filter out at least 95% of airborne particles in controlled testing conditions.

In other words, the letter classification—N, R, or P—tells you how well the mask resists oil-based particles. “N” means it’s not oil-resistant, “R” means it’s somewhat oil-resistant (think ‘resistant’), and “P” means strongly oil-proof (think ‘oil-proof’). The “95” part is about efficiency: an N95 mask filters out at least 95% of particles that are around 0.3 microns in size. For context, a human hair is roughly 50 to 70 microns wide—much larger than what N95 masks are designed to catch.

These test conditions are set by NIOSH, which is part of the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Before a mask can bear the N95 label, it must pass rigorous testing in their laboratories. “They run these masks through controlled experiments where air is pumped through the mask, and particle counts are measured before and after,” says Matt Powell, a product engineer at a personal protective equipment manufacturer. “If it consistently filters out at least 95% of the test particles, it earns that N95 rating.”

It’s worth noting that N95 masks are known as respirators rather than ordinary masks. While a simple cloth or surgical mask can help block large droplets, an N95 respirator creates a tight seal around the nose and mouth. This ensures that when you breathe, you’re pulling air through the mask’s filter, not through gaps at the edges. “That’s why getting the right fit is crucial,” Dr. Lee emphasizes. “If you don’t have a good seal, you’re not getting the full benefit of that 95% filtration.”

So why all the fuss about oil resistance? In many industrial settings, workers may be exposed to oily mists or aerosols. Oil-based particles can degrade the filtration material in some masks, making oil resistance an essential factor in certain workplaces. For the general public, especially in situations like a pandemic, what matters most is that 95% filtration figure—which helps protect against fine, airborne particles like dust, smoke, or certain pathogens.

In short, “N95” is more than just a label. It’s a code that explains exactly what the mask can do: filter out at least 95% of tiny airborne particles, as tested under strict conditions, though it won’t withstand exposure to oily aerosols. “Knowing what N95 stands for helps you understand why these masks are so effective,” says Dr. Lee. “They’re a proven, standardized form of protection—no guesswork required.”
title: What Does the N95 Stand for in N95 Masks?

When the temperatures drop and a chill settles in the air, few things comfort as quickly or deliciously as a steaming mug of hot chocolate. But as you wrap your hands around that warm cup, have you ever paused to wonder where this decadent drink originated?

“Chocolate beverages have a rich and ancient heritage,” says Dr. Carla Martin, a chocolate historian at Harvard University. Long before marshmallows were bobbing in sweet milky cocoa, chocolate was consumed by Mesoamerican civilizations. The Mayans and Aztecs of Central America drank a bitter, frothy concoction made from ground cacao beans mixed with water and spices like chili and vanilla. It was a far cry from the sugary treat we know today.

For these early chocolate drinkers, cacao beans weren’t merely a source of pleasure—they were valuable currency and held a sacred place in religious ceremonies. “Chocolate was considered a gift from the gods,” explains Dr. Martin, “and the drinks prepared from it were often consumed by nobility and warriors, believed to provide strength and vitality.”

It wasn’t until European explorers arrived in the Americas that chocolate would shift toward sweetness. When Spanish conquistadors returned home in the 16th century carrying cacao beans and chocolate-making knowledge, Europeans experimented by adding sugar, which had become more readily available. With this one adjustment, the bitter chocolate beverage evolved into a sweet indulgence that quickly spread throughout Europe’s upper classes.

By the 17th and 18th centuries, hot chocolate was a beloved luxury. In France, King Louis XIV’s court savored chocolate drinks at decadent gatherings. Across the English Channel, London’s chocolate houses—like early coffee shops—became fashionable meeting spots where people sipped rich hot cocoa and debated the issues of the day. “Europeans not only embraced chocolate,” says Sarah Mayfield, a food anthropologist in London, “they elevated it. It became associated with sophistication, conversation, and social status.”

As chocolate plantations expanded and production methods improved, prices began to drop, making hot chocolate more accessible. The Industrial Revolution further democratized chocolate, allowing it to be mass-produced and sold to the middle class. By the 19th century, drinking chocolate had crossed the Atlantic again, this time to the United States, where it continued to evolve. Americans refined recipes, sometimes using milk instead of water, yielding the creamy, comforting beverage we love today.

The modern version of hot chocolate most of us enjoy—often made with cocoa powder, sugar, and milk—would probably surprise an ancient Mayan. “It’s sweeter, smoother, and less spicy than the original,” Mayfield notes. “But the essence remains: it’s a comforting drink that warms both body and spirit.”

Today, hot chocolate is experiencing a renaissance. Artisan chocolatiers craft luxurious cocoa blends, and cafés offer gourmet hot chocolate flights featuring unique flavors from around the world. In wintertime, it remains a cherished treat for families, who top it with whipped cream or marshmallows and sip it by a crackling fire.

In many ways, hot chocolate’s journey mirrors our human story—adaptation, exchange of ideas, and the blending of old and new traditions. “With each sip,” says Dr. Martin, “you’re tasting centuries of history, cultural exchange, and innovation.” It’s a delicious reminder that sometimes the simplest pleasures carry the deepest roots.
title: The Delicious History of Hot Chocolate

For centuries, people have trusted the humble coin toss to settle heated debates, choose who goes first, or determine a winner. It’s easy to assume that flipping a coin is the most straightforward, unbiased method out there. After all, heads or tails seems like a 50/50 proposition. But recent research suggests that this age-old belief might not be entirely accurate.

“Most of us have grown up believing that a coin toss is perfectly fair,” says Dr. Persi Diaconis, a mathematician at Stanford University who has studied the mathematics of flipping coins. “However, once you begin to test the flips in a controlled setting, patterns start to emerge.”

One key insight from Dr. Diaconis’s work and other studies is that coins have a slight tendency to land on the same side they started on. In other words, if a coin is initially placed heads-up on your thumb, there’s a slightly better-than-even chance that it will land heads-up after the flip. While this bias might not be huge—some studies find it could be around 51% instead of a perfect 50%—it still challenges the notion of a perfectly even split.

What causes this subtle imbalance? It comes down to physics and human motion. When you flip a coin, you apply a certain force that sends it spinning through the air. No matter how hard you try to make your flips identical, there will be tiny differences in how fast and how straight the coin spins. Also, coins aren’t perfectly symmetrical—minute variations in weight distribution and the thickness of the metal can affect how they rotate and land.

“Even factors like which finger you use to flick the coin, the angle of release, and the height from which you flip can introduce bias,” explains Dr. Diaconis. “Over a large number of flips, these small differences add up.”

Interestingly, the belief in a fair 50/50 split is as old as the practice of coin tossing itself. The ancient Romans, for instance, used coin tosses—known as “navia aut caput” (ship or head)—to make quick decisions. Through the ages, people have relied on this simple method precisely because it seems unbiased, accessible, and easy to understand.

But now that we know there might be a slight tilt in the odds, should we abandon the coin toss altogether? Not necessarily. “For most everyday purposes—like deciding who washes the dishes—this tiny bias doesn’t really matter,” says Dr. Diaconis. “The small percentage difference won’t have much of an impact on your life, and the convenience of using a coin still outweighs the imperfection.”

If perfect fairness is crucial, however, consider alternative methods. Computerized random number generators, for example, can offer more reliable randomness. Or try shaking the coin in your hands before tossing it to reduce the bias of the initial side facing up.

In the end, while a coin toss may not be a perfectly fair 50/50 event, it’s still a good-enough method for most everyday decisions. The takeaway? Sometimes, even our simplest assumptions about chance need a closer look.
title: Think a Coin Toss Is 50/50? Think Again

text:
On a crisp morning, a highly educated professional might still hesitate before walking under a ladder on the way to the office. Another well-read individual may take special care not to open an umbrella indoors or might discreetly cross their fingers before a big meeting. These small rituals, easily dismissed as “just superstitions,” persist among people who otherwise trust in science, logic, and empirical evidence. It raises a fascinating question: Why do superstitions persist among seemingly rational individuals?

According to psychologists and anthropologists, the roots of superstition run deep in human history. “Superstitions are part of our evolutionary heritage,” says Dr. Stuart Vyse, a psychologist and author of *Believing in Magic: The Psychology of Superstition*. “They served as a buffer against uncertainty and potential danger in ancestral environments, where making a ‘safe bet’ could mean the difference between life and death.” While predators and immediate mortal threats may be less frequent in modern cityscapes, the underlying cognitive mechanisms that led to superstitious thinking still influence our behaviors today.

**The Evolutionary Underpinnings of Superstition**  
In the distant past, early humans faced myriad threats: predators lurking in the bushes, unpredictable weather patterns, scarce resources. Under these circumstances, our ancestors benefited from being overly cautious rather than missing a real danger. “In an uncertain environment,” explains Dr. Jane Risen, a behavioral scientist at the University of Chicago, “it’s better to make a mistake that costs little—like avoiding a certain spot because it seemed ‘bad’—than to ignore a potential warning sign that might result in injury or death.” This idea aligns with what evolutionary psychologists call “error management theory.” If making a superstitious assumption (such as associating a rustling in the grass with a lurking predator) kept our ancestors alive, even if the assumption was often wrong, then those who tended toward caution passed on their genes.

Over generations, this “better safe than sorry” attitude may have been woven into our cognitive fabric. While modern humans may not face saber-toothed cats, the brain’s tendencies remain. We still have a bias toward linking events that occur close together in time—like knocking on wood after expressing hope—to influence outcomes, even when logically we know there’s no causal connection.

**Pattern Recognition Gone Awry**  
Humans are natural pattern seekers. We look for meaningful connections in the world, finding order even where none exists. This capacity helps us learn and adapt—recognizing patterns leads to problem-solving and innovation. But when the desire to find patterns becomes too sensitive, we risk seeing connections where there are none. Superstitions often arise from this inclination. “If you wore a lucky shirt once and something good happened that day,” says Dr. Vyse, “your brain remembers that association. The next time you have an important event, you might put the shirt on again just in case.”

From an evolutionary standpoint, a false positive—believing that a meaningless action caused a good outcome—is less risky than a false negative—missing a real cause-and-effect relationship. As a result, our brains are wired to err on the side of caution, creating and maintaining superstitions that offer a sense of control over uncertain outcomes.

**Reducing Anxiety and Creating Control**  
One of the key reasons superstitions persist in the modern era is their ability to alleviate anxiety. Life’s uncertainty can be overwhelming, and superstitious rituals give people a feeling of control, even if it’s an illusion. “Performing a small, meaningful ritual can make people feel more at ease before facing a challenge,” explains Dr. Risen. “In high-stress situations—like taking a test or giving a presentation—a lucky charm or a ritualistic gesture can help calm the nerves.” This anxiety-reducing effect reinforces the behavior. After all, if you feel less stressed and more confident, you might perform better, which further cements the superstition in your mind.

This phenomenon is often seen in sports. Athletes at the top of their game, who rely heavily on training and skill, still follow pre-match rituals—eating the same meal, wearing a certain pair of socks, or performing a particular handshake with a teammate. These rituals don’t literally improve their performance, but they provide psychological comfort. “When an athlete hits a home run or scores a winning goal after following a ritual, the superstition is strengthened,” says Dr. Vyse. “It’s a powerful reinforcement loop.”

**Cultural Transmission of Superstitions**  
Superstitions also persist because they are passed down culturally and socially. As children, we absorb not only the language and customs of our community, but also its superstitions. Perhaps you watched your grandparents throw a pinch of salt over their shoulder to ward off bad luck. Or maybe your parents insisted that breaking a mirror would mean seven years of misfortune. These beliefs become ingrained through repetition and tradition, taking on a cultural significance that persists long after their original context is lost.

“Cultural evolution doesn’t always filter out irrational beliefs,” says Dr. Risen. “As long as the superstition isn’t harmful, it can survive for generations because it becomes part of the social fabric—something we do to feel connected to our past and our community.” In some cases, superstitions become a form of storytelling or folklore, adding richness and identity to a group’s shared history.

**The Modern Age of Information vs. Superstition**  
One might assume that in an age of abundant information, increasing education, and scientific progress, superstitions would fade away. Yet, they persist, sometimes even flourish. Part of the reason is that rational and irrational beliefs can coexist in the same mind. A person can trust modern medicine while still refusing to walk on cracks in the sidewalk or avoiding the number 13.

“In many cases, people compartmentalize their beliefs,” says Dr. Vyse. “They apply rational, scientific thinking in areas where it’s important—like their job or their health decisions—but preserve harmless superstitions as a kind of psychological comfort or cultural practice.” This duality allows intelligent, well-informed individuals to embrace rituals that have no logical grounding.

Another factor is that superstitions often thrive in areas of life where outcomes are uncertain and stakes are high—love, career success, health, or even financial markets. When confronted with uncertainty, even the most rational person might resort to a lucky gesture. “It’s a natural human response to situations we can’t fully predict or control,” says Dr. Risen.

**Overcoming or Embracing Superstitions**  
For those who find their superstitious habits bothersome or irrational, understanding why these beliefs persist can help break their hold. Recognizing that superstitions are a product of evolution, pattern recognition, and cultural tradition can strip them of some of their mystique. “When you see a superstition for what it really is—a harmless mental shortcut—it’s easier to let go,” says Dr. Vyse.

Still, many people choose to keep their superstitions. Provided they don’t cause harm or interfere with rational decision-making, these rituals can be seen as comforting quirks rather than flaws in logic. In fact, some psychologists argue that certain superstitions can have positive effects: they might reduce stress, increase confidence, or foster social bonds through shared practices.

“It’s not about eradicating superstitions completely,” says Dr. Risen. “Instead, we can aim to be aware of them, understand their origins, and use that knowledge to guide how we relate to them. If knocking on wood helps you relax before a big interview, that’s not necessarily a bad thing—just don’t rely on it as a substitute for preparation.”

**A Legacy Carried Forward**  
Superstitions persist among seemingly rational people because they reflect a fundamental aspect of our human nature: our brains are designed to find patterns, manage uncertainty, and reduce anxiety. They’re holdovers from a time when making the safer choice—whether it was truly logical or not—could mean survival. Today, superstitions often serve as small psychological boosts, comforting rituals, or cultural traditions that bind us together.

As we move further into a world guided by science and reason, superstitions will likely remain, whispering from the past. They remind us that, despite all our progress, we’re still creatures shaped by eons of evolution, searching for meaning and control in a complicated universe. And perhaps, in understanding that truth, we can appreciate these harmless quirks of human psychology for what they are: echoes of our history, woven into the tapestry of everyday life.

text:
When your child starts acting differently—getting lower grades, missing curfews, or developing concerning habits—it’s natural to wonder where the change is coming from. Often, parents find themselves pointing the finger at their child’s friends, dismissing these peers as a “bad influence.” This reaction, though common, can do more harm than good. Instead of saving your child from trouble, calling a friend a bad influence may actually push your child away, cause resentment, or even strengthen the bond you’re trying to break.

“Adolescents are navigating a stage in life where peer relationships are incredibly important,” says Dr. Lisa Damour, a psychologist specializing in adolescent development and author of *Untangled: Guiding Teenage Girls Through the Seven Transitions into Adulthood*. “When parents label a friend as a bad influence, it can feel like a personal attack on the teenager’s judgment and social life.”

**The Power of Peer Groups**  
It’s no secret that teens are influenced by their peers. Research has consistently shown that friendships help shape beliefs, behaviors, and identities. Yet the notion that a single “bad” friend is leading your child astray may be too simplistic. Dr. Damour points out that many factors contribute to a child’s actions—personality, family dynamics, mental health, and even broader cultural influences. Blaming an external peer downplays the complexity of adolescent development.

Moreover, labeling a friend this way can inadvertently validate your teen’s loyalty to that friend. “Adolescents value trust and support in their relationships,” explains Dr. Jess Shatkin, a child and adolescent psychiatrist at NYU Langone Health and author of *Born to Be Wild: Why Teens Take Risks, and How We Can Help Keep Them Safe*. “If they feel their parents are unfairly criticizing someone they care about, they’ll likely jump to their defense.”

**The Adolescent Brain and Loyalty**  
During the teenage years, the brain is in the midst of significant change. Adolescents are developing their own sense of identity, separate from their parents, and forging unique social networks. This process naturally involves testing boundaries, seeking acceptance, and learning to form independent judgments. When parents call a peer a bad influence, teens may hear this as a lack of trust. Instead of seeing their parents’ perspective, they may dig in their heels, clinging more tightly to the friend in question.

“Adolescents are establishing their autonomy,” notes Dr. Shatkin. “They want to prove that they can pick their own friends and make their own decisions. By criticizing their friend, you’re also criticizing their judgment, which can cause them to rebel.”

**Why Labeling Backfires**  
There are several reasons this labeling strategy can backfire:

1. **Defensiveness:** Teenagers often respond to negative judgments by becoming defensive. If you say, “Your friend is a bad influence,” your child might feel compelled to defend that friend, shutting down any productive conversation.

2. **Damaged Trust:** If your child sees your judgment as unfair, they may feel you don’t understand their social world. This can erode the trust between you and your teen, making it even harder to communicate about sensitive issues.

3. **Increased Secrecy:** Feeling that you’re unjustly attacking their friend could lead your child to hide information or distance themselves from you. They might spend more time with the very friend you disapprove of, simply because they feel misunderstood.

4. **Loss of Teachable Moments:** By pointing fingers at a peer, you miss an opportunity to discuss the real issues at hand, whether that’s the consequences of certain behaviors, the challenges of decision-making, or strategies for resisting peer pressure.

**A More Productive Approach**  
If labeling a friend is not the answer, what should parents do instead?

1. **Focus on Behaviors, Not People:** Rather than saying, “That friend is a bad influence,” try talking about the specific behavior that concerns you. For instance, “I’ve noticed you’ve been staying out past curfew when you’re with Alex, and I’m worried about your safety.” This shifts the conversation away from personal attacks and toward concrete actions and outcomes.

2. **Listen and Ask Questions:** Before making judgments, ask your child what they like about their friend. Understanding your teenager’s perspective can build empathy and trust. “Ask open-ended questions,” advises Dr. Damour. “What do you enjoy about your time with this friend? How do you feel after you spend time together? What makes them a good friend?” By listening, you show respect for your child’s social world, which can encourage them to be more receptive to your guidance.

3. **Express Concern, Not Blame:** If you’re truly worried about the friend’s influence, express that concern calmly and compassionately. Say something like, “I love you and I want you to be happy and safe. I’m worried that some of the things you’ve been doing lately—like missing assignments or skipping practice—might affect your future. Let’s talk about how to keep you on track.” By framing it this way, you focus on your child’s well-being rather than the supposed failings of their friend.

4. **Offer Alternatives and Solutions:** If you think certain situations with this friend lead to negative outcomes, brainstorm solutions together. Maybe they can hang out in safer environments or include another friend you trust. By collaborating, you help your child maintain agency while guiding them toward better choices.

5. **Set Clear Boundaries:** You can still set rules and expectations without demonizing their friend. For example, establish curfew times, academic standards, and household responsibilities. Explain that these rules apply regardless of who they’re spending time with. “Consistent boundaries help adolescents know where they stand,” says Dr. Shatkin. “It’s not about controlling their social circle; it’s about ensuring their overall well-being.”

**Building Long-Term Trust**  
Parenting adolescents involves a delicate balance between monitoring and independence, guidance and freedom. Navigating the complexities of their friendships can be tricky. Yet, treating your teen’s social world with respect and avoiding knee-jerk labels can make a significant difference.

“When parents take the time to understand why their children value certain friendships, even if they don’t fully approve, it creates an environment of trust,” says Dr. Damour. “In that environment, young people are more open to hearing their parents’ concerns and considering their advice.”

Over time, as your child grows into adulthood, the lessons they learn about friendship, loyalty, and responsibility will be shaped not just by their peers, but also by the way you handle these challenges. Instead of blaming their friends, emphasize your child’s capacity for good judgment, personal growth, and positive decision-making. Encourage them to reflect on their behaviors, think critically about their social interactions, and take responsibility for their choices. In doing so, you’ll help them develop the tools they need to navigate complex social dynamics—now and in the future.

**A Lifelong Skill**  
Ultimately, friendships are key sources of support, learning, and emotional development throughout life. By avoiding the simplistic label of “bad influence,” you empower your child to understand their relationships more deeply. They’ll learn to assess the pros and cons of their friendships, cultivate positive connections, and make better decisions without feeling attacked or misunderstood.

“In the end, helping your teen learn to judge character, set personal boundaries, and make healthy choices is far more valuable than placing blame on a friend,” Dr. Shatkin concludes. “These skills will serve them well into adulthood.”

By fostering open communication, focusing on behaviors rather than blame, and offering guidance without condemnation, you can help your child navigate their social world with confidence, integrity, and resilience—no matter who their friends are.
title: Parents Labeling a Kid’s Friend a Bad Influence Can Backfire

text:
For more than a century, a short story penned by Bram Stoker—famed author of *Dracula*—remained buried among the archives of the National Library of Ireland, overlooked and forgotten. Recently, an amateur historian and devoted Stoker enthusiast, Michael Flanagan, stumbled upon the lost tale while researching Victorian-era periodicals. The story, titled “Gibbet Hill,” now emerges as a remarkable literary discovery that sheds new light on Stoker’s early writing style and thematic interests.

“It’s not every day you find a piece of lost literature by a writer of Stoker’s caliber,” says Dr. Margaret O’Leary, a literary scholar at Trinity College Dublin who has examined the manuscript. “Stoker’s *Dracula* is rightly celebrated, but ‘Gibbet Hill’ suggests that his fascination with the macabre and the supernatural took root well before his magnum opus.”

Flanagan’s unexpected find occurred in the library’s reading room, where he was poring over obscure 19th-century magazines and newspapers. Among their brittle pages, he noticed a story with no byline but with a style reminiscent of Stoker’s distinctive Gothic tone—dark forests, eerie landscapes, and a quiet dread lurking at the fringes of everyday life. Curious, Flanagan dug deeper, eventually matching certain phrases and stylistic quirks to Stoker’s known works.

The National Library of Ireland confirmed that the story is indeed Stoker’s own. Librarians cross-referenced publication dates, printing styles, and editorial notes from the period. Although the exact date of writing remains uncertain, literary historians believe “Gibbet Hill” likely predates *Dracula* (published in 1897) by at least a decade.

“Gibbet Hill” tells the eerie tale of travelers who venture to an infamous spot known for its grisly past of public hangings. As night falls, eerie lights appear, and strange whispers fill the air. The story’s tension builds as the characters confront both external terrors and the darker corners of their own minds. While less polished than *Dracula*, experts say the narrative showcases Stoker’s early attempts to blend history, legend, and the supernatural into a cohesive, spine-chilling narrative.

“This discovery allows scholars to trace how Stoker’s voice evolved,” notes Dr. O’Leary. “We can see him experimenting with atmosphere and tension, refining narrative techniques that would later find their perfect expression in *Dracula*.”

The amateur historian’s find highlights the invaluable role enthusiasts can play in literary research. “I’m just a fan of Gothic literature,” says Flanagan. “I never dreamed I’d be the one to rediscover a lost work by Bram Stoker. It’s been an incredible journey—one that shows how much of our cultural heritage is still waiting to be found in archives.”

Now that “Gibbet Hill” has resurfaced, the National Library of Ireland plans to preserve and digitize the story, making it accessible to scholars and the general public. As it enters the literary conversation, the tale may offer fresh insights into Stoker’s influences, from Irish folklore to the Victorian fascination with death and the afterlife.

“History can hide remarkable treasures in plain sight,” says Dr. O’Leary. “With ‘Gibbet Hill,’ we have a new piece of the puzzle—a glimpse into the mind of a young Stoker honing his craft, quietly shaping the Gothic tradition that he would eventually transform forever.”
title: Amateur Historian Discovers Lost Story by ‘Dracula’ Author Bram Stoker Hiding in Plain Sight at a Dublin Library

text:
An upcoming Sotheby’s auction is making headlines, and not just because of the artwork or the subject it portrays. The featured piece—an abstract portrait of Alan Turing—is made by a robot named Ai-Da. Using a combination of artificial intelligence algorithms, cameras, and robotic arms, Ai-Da has produced what’s believed to be the first artwork created by a humanoid robot ever offered by the prestigious auction house. Experts estimate it may sell for as much as $180,000.

“Ai-Da represents a fascinating intersection of art and technology,” says Dr. Lucy Thomson, a digital art historian at the University of Oxford. “The fact that a robot can create something that humans recognize as art challenges our fundamental assumptions about creativity, authenticity, and the role of the artist.”

Named in honor of Ada Lovelace, the 19th-century mathematician often considered the first computer programmer, Ai-Da uses advanced AI algorithms to analyze visual input and translate it into brushstrokes. Special cameras scan the subject—or, in this case, existing images of Alan Turing—to form a digital understanding of shapes, contours, and colors. Based on this analysis, the robot’s software determines how to position the robotic arm and which brushstrokes to apply, resulting in an unpredictable yet striking final product.

Alan Turing’s legacy looms large over the fields of mathematics, computing, and artificial intelligence. He laid much of the groundwork for modern computer science and helped break the Nazi Enigma code during World War II. Capturing his likeness—albeit in an abstract form—using a robotic system that might not exist without Turing’s pioneering ideas adds a layer of poetic significance.

The artwork reflects more than just lines and colors; it’s a comment on the relationship between human ingenuity and machine capabilities. Critics and collectors alike are divided on what it means for a robot to create art. Is the robot’s “creativity” genuine, or is it a sophisticated extension of its human programmers?

“It’s a philosophical question,” says Dr. Thomson. “The painting wouldn’t exist without humans who built Ai-Da’s hardware, wrote her software, and curated the data fed into her algorithms. Yet the final product is something that emerges from the machine’s own learning process.”

Some argue that the very act of selling the painting at Sotheby’s suggests that the art world takes this robotic creation seriously. By placing it alongside artworks by human artists, the auction house is acknowledging the robot’s output as culturally and economically valuable. Whether that value holds over time will depend on evolving attitudes toward AI-generated art.

Ai-Da’s Turing portrait may not herald the end of human creativity, but it undeniably marks a new chapter. “As technology advances,” Dr. Thomson notes, “our definition of art and artist will continue to evolve. Ai-Da’s work invites us to consider what it really means to be human in the age of artificial intelligence.”

If nothing else, the upcoming sale will be a milestone. Whether the painting fetches $180,000 or more, it will stand as a symbol of how far we’ve come—and how far we may yet go—in blending art and science.
title: A Portrait of Alan Turing Made by an A.I.-Powered Robot Could Sell for Up to $180,000

text:
Today, it’s hard to imagine a world where a child’s bedroom shelf isn’t adorned with at least one teddy bear. This cuddly companion is nearly as iconic as apple pie and baseball in the American cultural landscape. Yet, when it first emerged in the early 1900s, the teddy bear was not universally embraced. In fact, some observers feared it would have a dangerous influence on the nation’s youth, challenging traditional notions of childrearing and morality.

The story of the teddy bear begins with a moment of surprising empathy from President Theodore Roosevelt. In 1902, Roosevelt participated in a bear-hunting expedition in Mississippi. After hours of fruitless search, guides captured a lone, wounded bear and tied it to a tree, inviting the president to make the kill. Roosevelt, refusing what he considered unsportsmanlike conduct, ordered that the animal be released. News of the incident spread quickly, inspiring a political cartoon in The Washington Post that depicted Roosevelt’s act of compassion. Soon after, Brooklyn-based toymakers Morris and Rose Michtom created a plush bear in honor of the president, labeling it “Teddy’s Bear.” Around the same time in Germany, the Steiff company produced its own line of jointed bears that would soon become popular worldwide.

“These bears quickly struck a chord,” says Dr. Sarah Cole, a cultural historian at Columbia University. “At a time when mass-produced consumer goods were on the rise, the teddy bear offered something warm, comforting, and relatable. Children loved them immediately, finding a sense of companionship in these furry toys.” Once the initial novelty wore off, however, not everyone shared this enthusiasm.

Early resistance to the teddy bear came from some parents, educators, and moralists who worried that the new toy would challenge traditional values. “It might seem strange today, but people argued that the teddy bear was too soft, too easy, and perhaps too indulgent,” explains Dr. Cole. “Children were supposed to learn through structured play, often with moralistic or instructional toys—dolls that taught social roles or books that conveyed moral lessons. A simple, cuddly bear didn’t fit that mold.”

Some commentators at the time warned that the teddy bear’s popularity would discourage children from playing with more ‘wholesome’ toys or reading morally uplifting stories. According to period letters and editorials, certain critics claimed that children were growing too attached to their plush pals, neglecting their chores, duties, and even their spiritual upbringing. “By snuggling up to a teddy bear,” says Cole, “some feared children would become soft in character, too reliant on comfort instead of building resilience and strength.”

Religious leaders, in particular, sometimes took aim at the bear. One sermon from the early 1900s railed against “the creeping influence of mindless amusements” and included plush bears as part of the problem. “Religious critics argued that traditional dolls, especially those resembling human babies or that came with miniature accessories, prepared children for adult responsibilities,” notes Dr. Ellen Carlow, a historian focusing on American childhood at the University of Pennsylvania. “A teddy bear was seen as morally neutral at best, and, at worst, a distraction from learning moral virtues.”

This moral panic over the teddy bear echoed broader societal anxieties of the time. The early 20th century saw rapid industrialization, urbanization, and shifting family dynamics. Mass consumer culture was emerging, with advertising and department stores suddenly able to sway tastes and trends. Parents, who had previously guided their children’s entertainment through handmade toys or carefully chosen storybooks, found themselves contending with a flood of commercial products. “In many ways, the teddy bear was a symbol of the new consumer age,” says Carlow. “It represented a break from homemade items passed down through generations. It was the product of factories, publicity, and popular culture.”

As the years passed, these fears began to wane. Children continued to love their teddy bears, and parents gradually accepted the toy as harmless—perhaps even beneficial. By the 1920s and 1930s, teddy bears had become part of the fabric of childhood. The idea that they were corrupting youth or undermining moral education faded away. Instead, the teddy bear started to serve new cultural functions: it was carried by soldiers going off to war as a token of comfort from home, given to hospital patients to soothe anxieties, and used by parents as a bedtime companion to ease fears of the dark.

“Over time, the teddy bear’s association shifted from moral threat to emotional support,” explains Carlow. “It became a tool for nurturing empathy, imagination, and security. What was once seen as potentially weakening a child’s character is now embraced as a gentle source of solace and reassurance.”

Today’s parents don’t typically question the presence of a teddy bear in the nursery. Instead, these plush animals are part of the essential landscape of childhood. Every so often, a new wave of worry about modern children’s play surfaces—fears that video games or smartphones might harm development. The teddy bear’s history reminds us that changes in childhood entertainment often spark anxiety, but those initial worries can fade as society adapts.

“The teddy bear’s early controversy teaches us that resistance to new forms of play is nothing new,” concludes Dr. Cole. “It underscores how cultural values and parenting ideals shift over time. What once was viewed as a dangerous influence is now a timeless symbol of comfort and care.”

In the end, the teddy bear emerged from its rocky start stronger than ever. By surviving the initial criticisms, it carved out a lasting place in our hearts, proof that a simple plush toy can carry immense cultural weight—and offer quiet warmth in an ever-changing world.
title: The Teddy Bear Was Once Seen as a Dangerous Influence on Young Children

On the rugged shores of New Zealand’s southeastern coast, the yellow-eyed penguin, or **hoiho**, is facing a dire struggle. The species, known for its distinctive, pale-yellow eyes and shy demeanor, has experienced steep population declines in recent decades due to threats like habitat loss, predators, and disease. Now, a team of dedicated scientists and conservationists is stepping in with extraordinary measures—ranging from hand-feeding “fish smoothies” to administering oral antibiotics—in a last-ditch effort to ensure the survival of one of the world’s rarest penguins.

“We’ve reached a critical turning point,” says Dr. Mel Young, a seabird ecologist at the Department of Conservation in New Zealand. “Without intervention, we risk losing this species entirely.” Once abundant along the country’s coastline, fewer than 3,000 yellow-eyed penguins are believed to remain. Their nesting sites have been disrupted by human development and introduced predators such as stoats and ferrets, while warming oceans have affected the availability of their preferred prey.

Conservationists have adopted a hands-on approach to boost penguin health and help fledglings reach maturity. This often involves rescuing underweight chicks and delivering nutrient-rich “fish smoothies”—a carefully blended mixture of fish fillets and essential supplements—to help them gain strength. “Feeding them directly ensures that they get enough calories and critical nutrients when the natural food supply is uncertain,” explains Dr. Young. “It’s like giving them a jump-start on life.”

In addition to nutritional support, the team has pioneered using oral antibiotics to treat and prevent the spread of respiratory infections that have plagued the population. Administering medicine to wild penguins isn’t easy; it requires gentle restraint and skillful delivery to avoid stressing the birds. “We’re essentially acting as their temporary guardians,” says Rachel Harrington, a wildlife veterinarian involved in the project. “Treating infections promptly prevents further weakening of the population.”

Beyond direct medical care, researchers are also focusing on environmental management. They are restoring native coastal vegetation to shelter the penguins’ nesting areas and installing predator-proof fences to ward off invasive species. “Habitat restoration and predator control go hand in hand with medical intervention,” Harrington notes. “We’re trying to address the root causes of their decline as well as treating immediate health issues.”

This unconventional, labor-intensive approach has already yielded some encouraging results. Over the past few breeding seasons, more chicks have survived to fledge, slowly stabilizing local populations. It’s a delicate balance—wild animals generally fare best without human interference, but the dire circumstances demanded action. “Ideally, we would want these penguins to thrive on their own,” Dr. Young explains. “But at this point, our involvement may be the difference between their survival and extinction.”

In the long run, the hope is that by improving conditions and bolstering penguin health, the species can rebuild robust populations without constant human care. “It’s about buying time,” says Harrington. “By offering a helping hand now, we give these remarkable birds a fighting chance to recover and, one day, stand on their own flippers again.”
title: How Scientists’ Tender Loving Care Could Save This Endangered Penguin Species

It’s easy to take your nose for granted—until you can’t use it the way most people do. For individuals born without a sense of smell, a condition known as congenital anosmia, the world is experienced differently. According to new research, that difference goes beyond missing out on aromas; it affects how they breathe, too. A recent study found that people with congenital anosmia sniff less often than those who can smell normally. The findings raise intriguing questions about whether this altered breathing pattern has any impact on overall health.

“Until now, most of us never thought about how the sense of smell might influence the way we inhale,” says Dr. Thomas Hummel, a smell researcher at the Technical University of Dresden Medical School, who was not involved in the study. “This research suggests that smell and breathing are connected more closely than we realized.”

In the study, published in the journal *PLoS ONE*, a team of researchers recruited participants with congenital anosmia—meaning they had never experienced scents—and compared them to a control group of people with fully functioning noses. During the experiment, participants were exposed to scent-related tasks and their breathing patterns were monitored using sensitive equipment.

The results were clear. Individuals with congenital anosmia sniffed less frequently and with less force than their peers. While people with a normal sense of smell often take quick, exploratory sniffs as they navigate their environment—sampling the air for clues about food, danger, or pleasant aromas—those born without smell didn’t show this behavior. “It’s as if the anosmic individuals had little incentive to engage in sniffing because they never get any sensory reward from it,” explains Dr. Maria Larsson, a psychologist at Stockholm University who studies the sense of smell and was not part of the research team.

Breathing through the nose does more than just detect scents. Air passing through the nasal passages is warmed, filtered, and humidified before it reaches the lungs. Specialized cells in the nasal cavity can help protect against pathogens, and the act of sniffing may even play a role in sharpening our attention to the environment. Without the instinctive urge to sniff, could individuals with congenital anosmia be missing out on these subtle benefits?

“That’s one of the big questions,” says Dr. Karyn Rhoads, the study’s lead author and a researcher at the University of Geneva in Switzerland. “We have established that their breathing pattern is different. Now, we want to know if that difference matters.” Could reduced sniffing impact respiratory health, immune function, or even cognitive aspects related to smell, like memory and emotion?

Previous studies have shown that smell has strong ties to emotion and memory. People often recall vivid personal experiences triggered by certain scents, and the lack of smell can alter how individuals relate to food, social interactions, and their own bodies. “Smell isn’t just a ‘bonus’ sense—it’s fundamental to how we perceive and engage with the world,” notes Dr. Larsson.

Still, having congenital anosmia is not necessarily harmful. Many people lead full, healthy lives without ever knowing the scent of roses or fresh bread. The next phase of this research will examine whether reduced sniffing leads to any measurable health differences. For instance, are these individuals more or less prone to nasal infections? Does the absence of smell-driven sniffing change the brain’s response to breathing or influence stress and relaxation?

More work is needed to uncover such connections. Future studies may compare lung function, sleep quality, or the incidence of respiratory conditions between people with congenital anosmia and the general population. Researchers might also investigate whether training or therapies aimed at mimicking normal sniffing patterns could offer any benefits.

For now, the findings serve as a reminder that even the most seemingly automatic behaviors—like breathing—can be influenced by our senses. “We’re learning that smelling and breathing are intertwined in ways we never fully appreciated,” says Dr. Hummel. “This research opens up a new perspective on what it means to live without smell. It’s not just about what they can’t sense; it’s also about how their bodies respond to a scentless world.”

In the end, the study provides a glimpse into the complex interplay between the senses and our basic bodily functions. Understanding these nuances could eventually lead to better support for people with congenital anosmia, ensuring that differences in breathing patterns don’t translate into hidden health disadvantages.
title: People Born Without a Sense of Smell Have Different Breathing Patterns, Study Finds

In the years before the United States fully established its own mint, colonial America relied on paper currency printed by a handful of skilled artisans. Among them was Benjamin Franklin, a man better known for his scientific discoveries, political influence, and witty aphorisms. Yet Franklin also played a pivotal role in safeguarding early American paper money against counterfeiters, employing ingenious techniques that combined artistry, materials science, and a keen understanding of human nature. Now, new research is shedding light on just how clever these early anti-counterfeiting measures really were.

A recent study, published in the journal *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences*, reveals that Franklin and his network of printers used a complex array of pigments, minerals, and fibers in their bills, making it nearly impossible for would-be forgers to replicate them exactly. By analyzing the chemical composition of surviving currency, scientists have identified unique “fingerprints” that made each note distinctive.

“Franklin was ahead of his time,” says Dr. Will Fleischer, a materials scientist at the University of Delaware who was not involved in the study but reviewed its findings. “He understood that reliable currency was essential to building public trust in the economy. Counterfeiting undermines that trust, so he tackled the problem at its source: the materials and methods used to print the bills.”

One of the key obstacles Franklin faced was the relative simplicity of early printing technology. Anyone with a press, ink, and paper could, in theory, attempt to copy a banknote. But Franklin’s genius lay in making replication far more difficult than it looked. He and his fellow printers experimented with adding unusual ingredients to their inks and papers, ranging from finely ground minerals to plant fibers of unique textures and colors.

According to Dr. Maria Nugent, a historian at the American Antiquarian Society, Franklin’s approach blended his scientific know-how with his printing expertise. “Franklin was a printer by trade before he became a statesman,” Nugent explains. “He understood the printing process intimately, and he applied that knowledge to money production. By using unexpected materials, he ensured that genuine bills had properties that counterfeiters wouldn’t anticipate, let alone easily recreate.”

To uncover these hidden characteristics, the research team employed modern analytical techniques, including X-ray fluorescence and scanning electron microscopy. These methods allowed the scientists to peer into the microscopic structure of the bills, identifying the chemical signatures of pigments and minerals. They discovered that certain natural dyes, sourced from specific regions, and particles of mineral-based pigments created a distinctive palette. Not only did these pigments give the currency its characteristic appearance, but they also provided subtle clues that the bills were authentic.

“In some cases, the paper itself contained tiny fibers from plants that didn’t grow just anywhere,” says Dr. Ellie Brooks, lead author of the study and a chemist at the University of Notre Dame. “This would mean that a counterfeiter—likely working under time and resource constraints—would struggle to find the exact same materials. The complexity of the supply chain for Franklin’s materials gave the legitimate currency a built-in security feature.”

Beyond the chemical and mineral composition, Franklin also experimented with ornate imagery and intricate woodcuts on the bills. These detailed patterns acted as an additional layer of protection. If a note’s design was extremely elaborate and drawn from a unique, handcrafted engraving plate, simply copying it with rudimentary tools would be nearly impossible.

“Franklin’s currency printing was essentially an early form of what we’d now call ‘security printing,’” says Nugent. “In the modern world, we use watermarks, holograms, and embedded microchips. Franklin used what he had: locally sourced materials, skilled engraving, and clever distribution of pigments. He turned natural scarcity into a security measure.”

While the main goal was to deter counterfeiters, these techniques had a broader cultural and economic impact. Reliable currency supported the growth of commerce and allowed early Americans to conduct business with greater confidence. The success of Franklin’s anti-counterfeiting measures meant that people could trust the value of the bills, even when precious metals were in short supply or prohibitively expensive.

“Stable currency is a cornerstone of any emerging economy,” notes Dr. Fleischer. “By preserving the integrity of their money, Franklin and his contemporaries helped foster an environment where commerce could flourish. It’s a subtle but crucial factor in the eventual success of the American experiment.”

Looking back, it might seem quaint that ground minerals and plant fibers once served as cutting-edge security features. But the core principle—making a counterfeit so challenging that it’s not worth the criminal’s effort—remains central to protecting currencies today. The difference is that modern technologies involve synthetic fibers, color-shifting inks, and even embedded electronics. Franklin’s solutions were no less clever; he simply used the tools available to him.

As Dr. Brooks reflects, “Franklin was famous for saying, ‘An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.’ In this case, preventing counterfeiting at the design stage was infinitely easier than tracking down and prosecuting counterfeiters after the fact. His approach still informs how we think about security today.”

In other words, the same mind that discovered electricity’s secrets and played a key role in shaping a young nation also left a legacy in something as seemingly mundane as paper money. Through the artful blending of pigments, minerals, and fibers, Franklin forged a financial system that was harder to fool, setting a precedent that still holds true in the modern era.
title: How Benjamin Franklin Helped Foil Early American Money Counterfeiters

text:
A San Francisco startup aiming to help dogs live longer, healthier lives has just raised $45 million in funding, highlighting a growing interest among venture-capital firms in longevity technologies—this time, not just for humans. The company, named Loyal, is developing drugs intended to slow the effects of aging in dogs and, if successful, could open the door to new approaches in age-related care for pets.

“We love our dogs like family members,” says Celine Halioua, Loyal’s founder and CEO, “but they simply don’t live as long as we want them to. At Loyal, we’re trying to address the underlying biology of aging so that our pets can enjoy more happy and active years with us.”

Founded in 2019, Loyal has drawn attention from high-profile investors as the pet industry continues to expand. According to the American Pet Products Association, Americans spend more than $100 billion a year on their pets, reflecting a strong appetite for products and services that improve animal health and longevity. With this latest round of funding, Loyal plans to continue its research, run clinical trials, and prepare the groundwork for bringing its first products to market.

The startup’s core idea is to develop pharmaceuticals that target the biological mechanisms of aging. Instead of addressing one disease at a time—such as arthritis or heart conditions—Loyal hopes to treat aging itself as a risk factor for multiple diseases. If successful, the drugs could extend not only the length of dogs’ lives, but also the quality of those extra years.

Dr. Matt Kaeberlein, a longevity researcher at the University of Washington who is not affiliated with Loyal, notes that the concept of treating aging as a medical condition is gaining traction in the scientific community. “The past decade has shown us that aging is modifiable,” he says. “If we can slow down the aging process, we may be able to significantly reduce the incidence of age-related diseases. Doing this for dogs is an appealing and achievable first step, given their relatively short lifespans and the strength of owner interest.”

Venture-capital investors have been paying close attention. While several longevity startups focus on human aging, the pet market offers a unique entry point. Dogs have shorter lifespans than people, meaning that clinical trials can yield data more quickly. The pet health market is also less strictly regulated than human pharmaceuticals, potentially speeding up the time it takes for a product to reach consumers. “Investors see an opportunity to generate returns while contributing to a growing field with vast potential,” says Mark Davies, a biotech investment analyst.

Loyal’s funding round places it among a cohort of longevity-focused startups that have recently raised significant capital. These companies aim to tap into a future where therapies could prevent or slow degenerative conditions across species. Some industry watchers believe that if these therapies are successful in dogs, the lessons learned could guide similar approaches for human medicine. “There’s a lot we can learn about aging from animal models,” Dr. Kaeberlein explains. “Dogs share our environment and many of our health risks, making them an ideal species to study.”

Still, the journey from concept to commercialization is long. Drug development is fraught with uncertainty, clinical trials can take years, and not every promising idea leads to a safe and effective product. Loyal must navigate a complex web of scientific, regulatory, and market challenges. “It’s one thing to prove something works in a laboratory setting,” says Davies, “and another to demonstrate safety, efficacy, and reliability at scale.”

For now, Loyal’s investors remain optimistic. The funding round, led by prominent venture firms, suggests that even with the known challenges, the company’s approach resonates with those holding the purse strings. “We look for investments that can reshape markets,” says an unnamed investor involved in the deal. “If Loyal’s approach pans out, it could fundamentally change how we think about pet health and aging.”

In the meantime, pet owners eagerly follow these developments. While it may be several years before a longevity treatment hits store shelves or veterinarians’ offices, the idea that science could help extend the time we spend with our furry friends is appealing. “Dogs bring us so much joy,” says Halioua. “Why not give them the healthiest, longest lives we can?”

As research continues, Loyal’s latest funding round signals a broader shift in how we view aging—not just as an inevitable decline, but as a biological process we might someday influence. For dogs, and perhaps one day for humans, that shift could mean more vibrant years together.
title: Dog Longevity Startup Loyal Secures $45 Million in Funding

text:
In the weeks leading up to Halloween, the usually staid corridors of the Southern District’s courthouse undergo a peculiar metamorphosis. Law clerks, administrative staff, paralegals, and even bailiffs transform their offices into full-blown haunted spectacles, vying for top honors in an annual competition that has become legendary within the legal community. Presided over by actual judges from the bench—men and women more accustomed to weighing complex legal arguments than cardboard skeletons—the contest is equal parts team-building exercise and spooky spectacle.

“The first time I judged it, I was speechless,” says Judge Lauren Garcia, who’s presided over more than a decade of homicide and white-collar crime cases. Yet it was the courthouse’s annual Halloween contest that nearly rattled her nerves. “I’ve handed down life sentences, heard testimony in harrowing criminal trials, and decided cases that would make most people’s heads spin,” she says. “But I don’t know if I’ll ever be as traumatized as I was then.”

The rules of the contest are simple enough: each department or office unit can decorate their area however they like, as long as it’s safe, respectful, and not interfering with daily operations. On the appointed day, a panel of judges—drawn from the district’s federal bench—tours each spooky-themed office. The judges then rate the displays on creativity, execution, and the sheer ability to startle. The trophy? Bragging rights and an office-wide reputation for theatrical flair that can last until the next October.

“It started out modestly about ten years ago,” says Joyce Mitchell, a court clerk who has worked in the Southern District for over two decades. “One office brought in a couple of plastic tombstones and some fake cobwebs. Another hung up a few papier-mâché bats. But then, year after year, it just got bigger and bigger. Now people plan their themes months in advance.”

This year, the themes ranged from classic haunted mansions to disturbingly realistic re-enactments of crime scenes that would feel at home in a thriller novel. A team from the records department created a “Zombie Legal Archive,” complete with dusty old ledgers and animatronic zombies rifling through case files. Across the hall, the finance unit converted their cubicles into a “Vampire’s Lair,” with red lighting, gothic candelabras, and a chilling soundtrack that played over hidden speakers.

“You’d think lawyers and clerks would be too practical to go all-out,” remarks Dr. Jamie Connors, a workplace culture expert at the University of California, Berkeley, who’s studied team-building activities in professional settings. “But in high-stress environments, events like this can actually help reduce tension. People have an outlet for creativity and humor, and that can translate into better morale and stronger working relationships.”

Judge Leonard Caldwell, who joined the bench only last year, recalls his initiation into the contest. “They told me I’d have to judge a Halloween competition,” he says, smiling wryly. “I thought it might be a few homemade costumes and some candy in bowls—maybe a joke pumpkin or two. Instead, I was led into what felt like a Disney-quality haunted house, except it was one floor of a federal building.” Caldwell confesses he had to stifle a yelp when a well-placed skeleton emerged from a hidden alcove. “You try maintaining judicial composure with a skeleton popping out of a file cabinet,” he chuckles. “It’s not easy.”

For the staff, these weeks of preparation don’t just build camaraderie—they also create an atmosphere of anticipation and fun that can actually improve work performance. “We’re proud of our jobs,” says Mitchell, “but it’s a serious environment most of the time. Preparing for the contest gives everyone something to smile about, to look forward to. After all, we’re working in the justice system, where stress can be high. Taking a break to hang some ghostly décor can do wonders.”

Not everyone embraces the event wholeheartedly, though. A few staff members find the competitive spirit daunting. “I admit, I felt pressure,” confides an assistant U.S. attorney who prefers to remain anonymous. “Our office’s theme didn’t win last year. It was a Viking-ghost cross-over idea that kind of confused people. This year, we decided on a simpler approach—just straight-up haunted courthouse. Fingers crossed it goes over well.”

Meanwhile, the judges face their own form of pressure. “We’re used to making weighty decisions based on law and precedent,” says Judge Garcia. “But here, what’s the standard? How do you fairly compare a ‘Mad Scientist’s Lab’ with a ‘Pirate Ghost Ship?’ There’s no manual for that. You have to rely on gut feeling—and maybe a sense of who startled you more.”

The judging process typically involves a clipboard with categories: originality, thematic consistency, level of detail, and yes, scare factor. “I’m usually not an easy scare,” says Judge Caldwell, “but I have to hand it to these staffers—they’re extremely inventive. One office tricked me into reaching for what looked like a coffee mug, only for a motion-activated ghoul to shriek in my face. I nearly dropped my pen.”

Despite the lightheartedness, the contest reflects something deeper about the court’s culture: it humanizes a place that the public often views as solemn and intimidating. “We’re all people,” says Garcia. “Judges, clerks, attorneys—everyone here is a human with interests and senses of humor. This contest lets us show that side to each other, reinforcing the fact that while we handle serious matters, we can also appreciate a good laugh.”

For the winning team, the reward is an inscribed plaque that stays in their department until next year. For everyone else, the fun lies in the process. And for the judges, it’s a reminder that even in a legal “house of horrors,” community and connection can thrive. “When I reflect on that first year I judged,” says Garcia, “I might say I was traumatized, but only in the most playful sense. It was a shock to the system—but a wonderful one.”

As the Halloween dust settles, the Southern District employees return to their briefs and hearings, their motions and rulings, quietly planning what spooky surprise they’ll whip up next year. “I can’t wait,” says Caldwell with a grin. “I’ll be ready for them. Or at least, I’ll try to be.”
title: In a Legal House of Horrors, It’s an Office Contest That Scares the Judges Most

text:
NASA will not return astronauts to the moon as soon as it had hoped. Officials confirmed this week that the first crewed landing under the Artemis program, originally planned for mid-decade, will be pushed back yet again—this time to no earlier than late 2026.

The revised schedule marks at least the third major shift since the White House set an aggressive target several years ago. Back then, NASA aimed for 2024, then slipped to 2025, and now acknowledges more time is needed. “We’re facing a combination of technical hurdles and budgetary pressures,” NASA Administrator Bill Nelson told reporters on Wednesday. “We have to be certain the systems are ready before we put our astronauts out there.”

Key hardware, including the Orion capsule and its European-built service module, as well as the massive Space Launch System rocket, has consumed more money and effort than forecast. NASA’s inspector general recently cited ongoing engineering problems, supply chain slowdowns, and the complexity of developing a lunar lander that can carry people safely down to the moon’s surface and back. SpaceX, tapped to provide that lander, has faced its own delays in testing and refining its Starship vehicle.

Critics in Congress are growing restless. Costs for Artemis have ballooned far beyond initial projections, and some lawmakers question whether NASA is doing enough to control spending. “NASA must provide clarity on what’s holding things up,” said Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., who sits on the House committee overseeing the space agency. “We need a plan that’s realistic and doesn’t keep shifting every couple of years.”

NASA officials insist that more time now will mean fewer problems later. Engineers still must verify how Orion’s heat shield performs during re-entry at lunar return speeds. The next uncrewed test flight, Artemis II, is currently on track for late 2024 or early 2025, after which NASA plans its first crewed trip around the moon without landing. That mission will give the crew a chance to evaluate life support and navigation systems in deep space before anyone attempts to set foot near the moon’s south pole.

“Human spaceflight is always hard,” said Dr. Cathy Koerner, who oversees Orion production. “The idea that we would land just a couple of years after finishing our first full test flights was always optimistic. It’s better to admit we need more time than to rush and regret it.”

Beyond the schedule concerns, international partners await a firm timeline so they can coordinate their roles. The European Space Agency supplies the Orion service module, and Canada is contributing a robotic arm for the planned Gateway station orbiting the moon. Japan is providing components for lunar surface logistics. These partners all rely on NASA’s roadmap to stay on schedule with their own hardware and training plans.

Some experts also warn that delays could open opportunities for other nations—particularly China—to catch up in the race to establish a foothold on the lunar surface. Beijing’s lunar plans include robotic sample returns and a future research station, raising the prospect of parallel efforts unfolding while NASA tackles its own setbacks.

For now, NASA is pressing ahead with the hardware it has and taking a hard look at what can be done to streamline the next steps. “We haven’t lost sight of the goal,” Nelson said. “But we won’t launch our crew until we’re confident this program can live up to its promise.”
title: NASA pushes back astronaut flights to the moon again

A half-dozen villagers in Napakiak, on the Kuskokwim River’s west bank, gathered near a gravel airstrip last Thursday to watch a small plane circle overhead. They weren’t expecting mail. No one around here bothers hoping for app-delivered groceries, not where single-engine aircraft and boats are the only ways in or out. This crowd was waiting for a seasoned pilot who had a tradition: dropping Thanksgiving turkeys to homes scattered across miles of tundra and frozen waterways.

The pilot, 47-year-old Alaskan flyer Erik Fosnes, has been doing this for nearly a decade, working with volunteers from a regional nonprofit called Delta North Outreach. “We tried shipping turkeys one year by cargo, but half never made it in time,” said Fosnes, running a hand through the frost on his jacket sleeve after landing. “So I said, ‘What if I just fly them in myself?’” He shrugged as if that were the most ordinary idea, then laughed. “Folks around here have gotten used to it.”

Because the villages along the lower Kuskokwim don’t have roads connecting them to Alaska’s highway network, residents rely on small aircraft or snowmobiles for most things. While some staples—rice, flour, coffee—are ordered through long-established supply lines, a fresh turkey is a different matter. With unpredictable weather and no year-round barge service, even a so-called “overnight delivery” can mean waiting a week or more. As far as something like a Thanksgiving bird is concerned, you can forget about big-name delivery apps. That’s where Fosnes steps in, cruising at low altitude and making quick stops to hand over carefully wrapped turkeys. When the ground is too soft or there’s no runway? He’s been known to attach a small parachute and drop the bird a short distance away from a waiting family—though he admits he tries to land whenever possible. “I’m not out here tossing them like water balloons,” he said, smirking. “We’re careful.”

In one village, Kokarmiut, people had set out fluorescent flags marking a clear patch on a riverbank. As Fosnes taxied to a stop, several residents trudged over, waving. Among them was Mary Attla, a teacher who grew up in the area. “We never had anything like this when I was a kid,” Attla said. “You’d get what you could—canned salmon maybe, something local. A turkey was a serious luxury.” She watched as a volunteer handed over a well-insulated box. “It’s not just about the food, it’s knowing someone bothered to show up out here. It makes the holiday feel like it matters.”

This year, the outreach group collected funds from donors in Anchorage and Fairbanks, and arranged for more than 200 frozen turkeys. Each bird weighed around 12 to 14 pounds—enough for a family meal plus leftovers. While rising fuel costs have made it more expensive to run these flights, Fosnes keeps doing it. He covers part of the cost himself and sometimes gets small donations of aviation fuel from local businesses. “I’m not some hero. I’m just a pilot who likes to help,” he said, adjusting the zipper on his flight jacket as the temperature dipped below freezing. “I know plenty of people who’d do the same if they had a plane and the time.”

Not everyone gets a turkey by plane. In a few spots, Fosnes relies on a friend driving a snowmachine over the tundra to meet him where the aircraft can’t safely land. In other areas, a local health clinic staffer or a traveling nurse takes custody of the turkey and ensures it reaches the intended household. It’s a patchwork system. “It’s definitely a bit improvised,” said Oliver Makar, a coordinator with Delta North Outreach. “We might call someone’s cousin two villages over, see if they’re heading that way. The goal is just to get that turkey to the family before the holiday. We manage somehow.”

Weather is always a gamble. On a recent run, heavy winds forced Fosnes to circle for half an hour above a coastal village before he felt confident enough to set down on a short airstrip carved out of tundra. “I’ve landed in some pretty questionable places,” he admitted, “but I won’t risk anyone’s safety. If I can’t land, maybe I’ll swing by the next day. People understand out here.”

Villagers appreciate this persistence. In small communities where even the closest grocery store might be a hundred miles away, having a turkey delivered by plane makes the feast feel special. “It’s an event,” said Ilona Pausuk, who lives near Kasigluk. “I remember the first time I saw Erik’s plane. Kids were yelling, ‘The turkey pilot is here!’ The next day, we cooked a meal with my mother and my aunt, and I swear it tasted even better because we knew how far it had come.”

The effort also reflects a long history of Alaskans helping each other out in remote corners. Just as communities band together when a storm hits or when the salmon run is poor, they rally around holiday traditions. “It’s not about charity,” Pausuk said, “it’s about connection. We see him year after year, and it reminds us we’re not forgotten.”

Fosnes shrugged off any grand interpretation. Standing near his Piper Super Cub, he checked his fuel gauge and fiddled with a map tucked inside his jacket. “I like flying. I like seeing people smile,” he said. “If a turkey can do that, then I’m game.” Then, with a quick wave, he climbed back into his cockpit. The propeller whirled, and in a moment the plane was airborne, heading off to the next village—a holiday messenger who would never dream of charging a delivery fee.
