A slim whale’s body, about five meters long, now rests on a stainless steel table at a marine laboratory near Wellington, New Zealand. Just a few days ago, it washed ashore on the Mahia Peninsula, puzzling locals who had never seen anything quite like it. Now, surrounded by a small team of researchers and cultural advisors, this pale, slender creature is at the center of a delicate examination that may finally help scientists understand one of the ocean’s most elusive mammals: the spade-toothed whale.

So rare is this species (formally known as Mesoplodon traversii) that it has never been spotted alive. Until now, scientists have only encountered it as partial remains—bones or fragments of tissue that turned up on remote beaches without any witnesses. Those rare finds have been enough to prove the whale exists, but not nearly enough to answer basic questions about its behavior, diet, or deep-sea habitat. That may be about to change, thanks to a carefully managed dissection currently underway.

“This is the first time we’ve had a fresh spade-toothed whale specimen that’s intact,” said Dr. Melissa Reid, a marine biologist with Te Herenga Waka—Victoria University of Wellington. “We’ve been working off stray jawbones and incomplete skulls for decades. To have a nearly complete individual right here in front of us, with tissues still preserved, is remarkable. This could rewrite what we know about the species.”

Before a single incision is made, there are protocols to follow that go well beyond standard scientific ethics. Whales hold a special place in Māori traditions and stories. Local iwi members have been involved from the start, ensuring the creature is treated with respect and that any samples taken follow a process that honors cultural values. A small group, including representatives from Ngāti Rongomaiwahine, stood alongside researchers as they prepared to begin.

“Whales are considered taonga—treasured beings. They connect us to our ancestors and our responsibilities to the sea,” said cultural advisor Merenia Paora, who has guided the research team through the proper rituals. “Our role is to ensure that, even in death, this whale is acknowledged for its significance, and that what we learn is shared thoughtfully.”

While the tension in the room is palpable, it’s not due to disagreements. Instead, there’s a collective awe. On the stainless surface are the telltale features that distinguish this whale from others: a pair of unusual, blade-like teeth that earned it the name “spade-toothed.” Hardly anyone has handled these teeth in a fresh specimen. Close by are syringes, sample jars, notebooks, and measuring tapes. In the corner, two cameras record the event to document every step for future research.

The team’s goals are modest yet groundbreaking. They will collect genetic samples, examine the whale’s inner ear bones to gauge its age, and look for clues in its stomach contents—perhaps revealing what it eats and how it might navigate the pitch-black depths of the ocean. They’ll take note of parasites, scars, or unusual tissues, hoping to find hints about whether these whales prefer certain water temperatures or if they travel alone or in small groups.

“We’re not expecting all the answers to pop out at once,” said Dr. Kevin Tan, a whale anatomist with New Zealand’s National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research. “But every sample and measurement we take is a piece of a puzzle that’s been missing for a century. Maybe we can finally learn if these whales feed mostly on squid, or if they have specialized diving adaptations like some of their close relatives. Even something as mundane as the thickness of their blubber can teach us how they survive in deep, cold water.”

The rarity of this moment is not lost on the scientists. Spade-toothed whales have been a kind of ghost species: confirmed on paper, but never observed breathing at the surface or diving below the waves. In 2012, when a mother and calf washed up, researchers knew they had struck scientific gold—but those specimens had already begun to decay, limiting what could be learned. Now, with a fresher whale, there’s a chance to extract higher-quality DNA and perhaps reveal subtle differences that separate these whales from others in the Mesoplodon genus.

“We’ve waited so long just for a chance like this,” said Reid, pausing with a scalpel in hand. “There’s a kind of responsibility here that we all feel. There aren’t many of these whales out there—at least, we assume they’re rare based on how few we’ve found. We must handle this with great care, and we want to share what we learn with everyone, including the communities that live along these coasts.”

In a few hours, the team will have extracted the needed samples. The whale’s remains, after consultation with the local iwi, may be buried or preserved in part for future study. The scientists will spend months—or even years—analyzing their data, writing up reports, and comparing notes with international colleagues who’ve been waiting for any scrap of new information on this mysterious species.

Meanwhile, the local community will remember the day a creature, unknown in life, became known through a respectful, painstaking investigation. “This whale may never have been seen swimming, but it hasn’t passed unnoticed,” said Paora. “Through this work, it will speak to us, helping us understand a corner of the ocean that’s been silent too long.”

Your phone buzzes with a last-minute work call, and you’re barely out the door. Meanwhile, Chester, your chocolate Lab, hovers near the entryway, ears drooped and pupils wide, looking as though his world might collapse when you twist that doorknob. It’s not just in your head—those pleading eyes can leave you feeling awful for even considering stepping outside without him.

It’s a scene that countless dog owners know too well. Whether it’s a two-hour errand or a full shift at work, leaving a beloved pet behind can spark waves of remorse. Social media platforms like TikTok and Reddit overflow with confessions from people who rearrange their schedules, adopt complicated kennel camera systems, or toss handfuls of pricey treats just to soften the blow of heading off without their canine companions. Jessica Lynn, a pediatric nurse in Milwaukee, says she sometimes lingers an extra ten minutes by the coat rack because her dachshund, Millie, “gives me that look—like I’m the absolute worst human on Earth for leaving.” Lynn tried giving Millie a puzzle feeder, but the dog’s intense gaze from the window still made her feel like a traitor.

That expression dogs wear—the so-called “puppy dog eyes”—is not some random fluke. Research suggests that domestic dogs have evolved distinct facial muscle structures that their wolf ancestors lacked. In a 2019 study led by comparative psychologist Juliane Kaminski at the University of Portsmouth, scientists found that modern dogs can raise their inner eyebrows more dramatically than wolves. This subtle muscle change transforms a dog’s face into what we interpret as sadness or concern. “We’re drawn to these signals because they mimic expressions we humans make when we’re distressed, so they tug at our empathy,” explains Kaminski. “It’s a brilliant evolutionary shortcut—dogs who could trigger nurturing responses from humans were likely favored over the centuries.”

The depth of the guilt we feel isn’t just about biology, though. Alexandra Horowitz, who heads the Dog Cognition Lab at Barnard College, points out that we often project human emotions onto our pets. “Your dog doesn’t necessarily ‘resent’ you for going to work,” says Horowitz. “But we read that feeling into their posture and their eyes. In reality, they’re reacting to cues we’ve taught them—like grabbing the car keys or putting on shoes—signals that mean you’re about to vanish for hours.” To the dog, it’s change and uncertainty, not moral judgment. Still, from the owner’s perspective, it’s hard not to interpret that posture and stare as a silent plea: Don’t leave me here alone.

This emotional tug-of-war can shape human behavior in measurable ways. Retailers have noticed a market for “guilt-reducing” products—elaborate feeders, automatic treat dispensers, toys that mimic a human’s heartbeat. Chewy.com, for instance, sells interactive cameras that toss treats at scheduled intervals, so owners can soothe their conscience by handing out snacks remotely. “We’ve seen a steady uptick in these devices,” says Ethan Miles, a product manager at a major pet supply chain who preferred not to name his company. “It’s not just about keeping your dog occupied—it’s a way for owners to feel less rotten about going grocery shopping or heading to the gym.”

Despite these technological props, many owners still carry the weight of leaving their pets behind. Christine Levy, who manages a dog-walking service in Philadelphia, has witnessed how people try to compensate for that lingering guilt. “I’ve seen clients run through complex rituals,” Levy says. “They’ll set the radio to classical music, drizzle chicken broth into a chew toy, or even FaceTime the dog from their office bathroom. It’s heartfelt, but it also reveals how deeply dogs’ expressions affect us. You’d think the person was leaving their kid at daycare for the first time, not just stepping out to pick up dry cleaning.”

So do dogs understand the impact of their gaze, or are we simply reading too much into their body language? Clive Wynne, who directs the Canine Science Collaboratory at Arizona State University, suggests that dogs quickly learn that certain looks yield owner attention. “They’re extremely good at reading our reactions,” says Wynne. “If whining softly at the door results in the owner putting down their briefcase and scratching their ears, they’ll do it again. They’re not plotting to guilt-trip you in a human sense—they’re just adept at noticing what works.”

This feedback loop can leave owners stuck, torn between the day’s responsibilities and their dog’s disappointed face. It also prompts serious questions about how we arrange modern life with companion animals who, at times, seem emotionally dependent. While canine experts say most healthy dogs cope just fine if their owners provide a safe environment and a consistent routine, the owners themselves may still feel uneasy. “You have to remind yourself that your dog’s momentary disappointment isn’t a moral failing,” Kaminski adds. “If they have food, water, a comfy spot, and eventually learn that you always come back, they adapt. They nap, they play with their toys, they move on.”

Some owners implement small rituals to ease their anxiety. Horowitz suggests a steady pre-departure routine—like a quick game of fetch or a predictable, gentle farewell phrase—so the dog associates leaving with a calm, normal pattern. “Dogs thrive on consistency,” she says. “Knowing what’s about to happen can lessen their confusion, and in turn, you might feel less bad about walking out.”

And sometimes, owners learn to embrace their feelings rather than chase them away. Jenny Wong, a graphic designer in Seattle, admits she still feels “a twist of guilt” when her golden retriever’s eyes follow her as she reaches for the keys. But she’s discovered that leaving on a more confident note—offering a cheerful goodbye and stepping out quickly—helps both parties. “If I linger, looking all mopey and apologizing, my dog actually seems more unsettled,” she says. “The quicker I go, the sooner he gets on with his day. I guess my guilt doesn’t help either of us.”

For many, that realization is the key. The sad eyes might never lose their power completely, but owners can learn to manage their reactions—ensuring that while their dogs have evolved to pull at our heartstrings, we’re still able to get on with our lives.
title: The Real Impact Those Sad Puppy Dog Eyes Have on Their Owners

When Michael Andrews first started tinkering with the shape of a beer glass, he didn’t set out to rewrite the rules of serving a proper pint. But after months of testing and a battery of computational models, Andrews — a mechanical engineer at the University of Bristol — says he may have determined a glass shape that can keep beer cooler longer than the familiar straight-sided or tulip designs on every pub’s shelf.

Andrews, who initially studied fluid mechanics in industrial pipelines, decided to apply his skills to something closer to home: British ales and continental lagers. “I was just curious whether minor tweaks to a glass’s profile could reduce heat transfer,” he says. “If you can control how quickly the head settles or how the beer circulates as you sip, maybe you can slow warming by a minute or two.”  

To test his idea, Andrews 3D-printed a series of experimental glasses, each with subtle variations: some flared at the top, others narrowed just before the rim, and a few incorporated a ribbed interior. He then poured a standard pale lager chilled to about 5 degrees Celsius into each prototype, monitoring how quickly the temperature rose under typical indoor conditions.

According to Andrews, the best-performing glass was shaped like a slightly tapered cylinder with a gentle inward curve near the lip. “I wouldn’t call it exotic,” he says, “but the angle and curvature slowed the rate at which the beer’s surface area interacted with warmer air.” In other words, less surface contact meant less heat gain. In tests, beer in this refined shape warmed at roughly 40% the rate seen in standard straight-sided pint glasses.

The study, published in the journal Fluid Dynamics Letters, has raised an eyebrow or two in the brewing community. “We’ve always believed that glass shape matters mainly for aroma release,” says Sarah Carmichael, head brewer at Little Finch Brewing in Leeds. “But hearing that a subtle contour shift might keep the beer colder a bit longer is intriguing.” She admits she’s not likely to redo all her glassware overnight, but she’s curious enough to run a few trials on her own taps.

Meanwhile, bartenders at The Crown & Anchor, a well-worn London pub catering to locals and university students, offered a more grounded perspective. “Most customers don’t fuss about a tenth of a degree,” says James Holt, who’s pulled pints there for nearly a decade. “If it’s fresh and well-kept, they’re happy. But if there’s a new style of glass that helps maintain flavor and temperature just that extra bit, I could see some folks asking for it.”

Andrews doesn’t expect widespread adoption anytime soon — after all, tradition and branding run deep in the beer world. Still, he imagines that some craft breweries or specialty bars might pick up the idea, especially for seasonal lagers or delicate ales best enjoyed at a stable temperature. “I’m not claiming a miracle,” he says, shrugging slightly, “just a neat reminder that physics can still tweak something as familiar as a pint of beer.”

text:
Anyone walking through the seed vaults at the International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center (CIMMYT) in Mexico might notice boxes labeled with dates that seem to belong in a museum. Inside are wheat seeds collected decades ago, some more than a century old. Though these seeds don’t look like much — small, brown kernels that fit in the palm of your hand — they represent genetic lineages that plant breeders say may hold the key to feeding people in a future marked by unpredictable climates, stubborn pests, and shifting demands.

Unlike many of today’s popular wheat varieties, some of these century-old strains come from an era before industrial agriculture standardized fields with a handful of high-yield lines. These older seeds were often gathered from small farms in places like Turkey or the edges of the Mediterranean, or passed down through communities in the U.S. and Canada that planted “Turkey Red” wheat brought by immigrant families. They carry traits shaped by local conditions that modern wheats may have lost — such as better tolerance to extreme heat, unusual resistance to fungal infections, or the ability to thrive on poorer soils.

“Back in the early 20th century, farmers planted wheat varieties we’d barely recognize today,” says Dr. Alison Bentley, who leads the Global Wheat Program at CIMMYT. “They didn’t always have the highest yield potential by modern standards, but they survived in tough conditions. Our goal is to rediscover what made them so resilient.” In other words, old wheat might not look glamorous, but it could quietly store genetic solutions to looming agricultural problems.

These days, wheat breeders aren’t just worried about delivering a bumper harvest under ideal conditions; they’re searching for varieties that can handle volatile weather patterns and spreading pathogens. Take the fungal disease known as stem rust. Some modern wheats are highly vulnerable, and outbreaks in Africa and other regions have threatened to wipe out entire fields. Meanwhile, older wheat lines stored in seed banks and once grown in modest family plots in Asia or Eastern Europe sometimes show strong rust resistance, thanks to genes honed over generations of low-input farming.

Scientists are also on the lookout for drought tolerance. With climate forecasts suggesting drier conditions in key wheat-producing areas, relying on a narrow genetic base could be risky. “Diversity isn’t a luxury, it’s a necessity,” says Dr. Matthew Reynolds, a wheat physiologist at CIMMYT. “Think of these old lines as our insurance policy. We might find a drought-tolerant gene in a variety that no one’s grown commercially since before the First World War.”

Seed banks around the world — including the Svalbard Global Seed Vault, Kew’s Millennium Seed Bank in the U.K., and CIMMYT’s own collections — hold tens of thousands of wheat samples. Many were tucked away in the mid-1900s, when collectors roamed local markets and field edges, scooping up seed from farmers who grew what their grandparents had grown. At the time, no one anticipated that researchers decades later would be cracking open these archives to rescue traits lost in the quest for uniform, high-performance crops.

To actually get these old varieties back into fields, breeders cross them with modern wheat, hoping to transfer beneficial traits without lowering yields too much. This isn’t a quick fix: It can take many breeding cycles and careful genetic screening to develop a new variety that farmers can realistically adopt. Sometimes you might find a gem right away; sometimes you spend years coaxing out a useful gene hidden amid a lot of genetic baggage.

In Canada, where wheat has long been a staple, researchers have looked back to historical lines like “Marquis,” a variety introduced in the early 1900s. Though it’s been eclipsed by modern wheat in terms of raw yield, breeders sifting through Marquis’s descendants have spotted disease-resistance genes that might shore up contemporary crops. And in parts of Ethiopia, scientists working with local institutes have rediscovered older landraces (ancient local varieties) that appear to handle fungal outbreaks more gracefully than standard commercial lines.

None of this is easy. Crossing old wheats with new ones can reintroduce unwanted traits, like weaker straw that causes plants to collapse under heavy grain heads, or grain that’s harder to mill into fine flour. Even after breeders identify a promising trait in an old seed, they must spend years refining it. Funding and patience are required, which isn’t always guaranteed.

Still, the urgency is evident. The global wheat trade recently faced disruptions from war in Ukraine and extreme weather in major producing regions. When regions that rely heavily on wheat imports see shortages, it’s a reminder that global food security isn’t theoretical. As demand grows with the world’s population, and climate swings become less predictable, a lack of genetic diversity could mean serious trouble.

“If we keep planting the same few varieties over and over, we’re asking for trouble down the line,” says Dr. Bentley. “It’s not about nostalgia. It’s about ensuring that in 50 or 100 years, we still have wheat that can feed people.”

Old seeds may not grab headlines like cutting-edge gene editing or vertical farming schemes, but they’re quietly reshaping how we think about the future of bread. As breeders tap into their ancestral genetic toolbox, 100-year-old wheat and its humble seeds stand ready to offer some fresh hope. No one said it would be simple, but few in the field doubt that these forgotten genes have something important to offer.
title: 100-Year-Old Wheat Could Help Feed the World

It started as a baffling finding by a team of Brazilian marine biologists who were studying the health of coastal shark populations near São Paulo State’s port regions. In a recent survey of Brazilian sharpnose sharks (Rhizoprionodon lalandii), the researchers detected trace amounts of cocaine metabolites in the animals’ tissues. While the study is still undergoing peer review, the initial results left the scientists at a loss: How could a reef-dwelling predator end up with narcotics in its body?

The emerging theory points to human activity along the coast. Illegal drug-production labs and trafficking routes dotting some Brazilian coastal zones may be discharging chemical byproducts into streams, estuaries, and bays that feed into the ocean. These compounds can persist in coastal ecosystems, mixing with sediment and plankton, and eventually moving up the food web to top predators like sharks.

**Unwelcome contaminants**

“These sharks aren’t nosing around shipping containers filled with contraband,” says Dr. Ricardo Melo, a marine toxicologist at the Federal University of São Paulo who supervised the study. “They’re picking up contaminants from their environment, probably from smaller fish that have already absorbed these chemicals.”

The Brazilian sharpnose shark, no more than two feet long and commonly found in shallow, coastal waters, feeds on shrimp, small fish, and cuttlefish—all of which can accumulate trace pollutants. If wastewater or runoff carries cocaine and related compounds from clandestine production sites or drug-lab discard piles, these substances could make their way through rivers and canals into coastal feeding grounds. Over time, even low concentrations can build up in predators.

The team conducted tissue analyses on several dozen sharks caught as bycatch in artisanal fisheries near Santos and Guarujá. Although the concentrations found were low, they were well above any background levels the researchers expected. “We knew urban effluents sometimes carry pharmaceuticals like antibiotics or painkillers,” says Melo. “But cocaine byproducts were a surprise. It suggests something more nefarious is happening upstream.”

**Paths of pollution**

Illicit labs often dispose of unwanted chemicals in makeshift ways: dumping waste into nearby creeks, burying residues in dunes, or flushing liquids into sewage systems not equipped to filter out complex compounds. “If a small, illegal lab dissolves coca paste and flushes the remains, the wastewater treatment plant won’t remove all those molecules,” says Dr. Carolina Souza, a marine chemist at the University of Campinas who was not involved in the research. “Some fraction can escape into rivers and, eventually, coastal waters.”

Coastal fisheries and port areas near large cities can concentrate this pollution. Runoff from heavy rains might carry contaminated sediments into estuaries, where juvenile fish and crustaceans live. Over months or years, these nursery grounds turn into reservoirs of contaminants. By the time a shark feeds there, it is essentially ingesting a cocktail of chemicals from its prey.

**Health implications for sharks**

Detecting cocaine in a shark might seem bizarre, but what does it mean for the animal’s health and behavior?

While no one has done controlled experiments exposing sharks to cocaine, researchers can make cautious guesses based on studies of other species exposed to psychoactive compounds. “In fish, even trace amounts of certain pharmaceuticals can alter stress responses, feeding, or reproductive success,” says Dr. Ana Lima, a marine ecologist at the Brazilian Institute of Environment and Renewable Natural Resources (IBAMA). “We don’t know if sharks experience something similar with cocaine compounds, but it wouldn’t be shocking if these chemicals disrupted their normal physiology.”

For an apex predator, subtle behavioral shifts can have ripple effects. If contaminated sharks feed less efficiently or struggle to navigate, the entire food web could be affected. Changes in predator distribution and hunting success might alter the balance of prey species, impacting the local marine community.

**Potential harm beyond sharks**

The presence of cocaine residues in marine predators might also signal broader environmental degradation. Beyond sharks, other animals—sea turtles, dolphins, even seabirds—could be encountering these pollutants. Although large marine vertebrates grab headlines, the more immediate concern might be small invertebrates and planktonic organisms at the bottom of the food web.

“These contaminants can accumulate in tiny organisms first,” says Souza. “When shrimp and juvenile fish feed on contaminated plankton, the contamination moves up the chain. By the time it reaches a shark, you’ve got a biomagnified effect. It’s a red flag for the entire ecosystem, not just one species.”

**Tracing sources and solutions**

Local authorities are now looking for ways to pinpoint where the contamination originates. Some suspect small-scale processing labs hidden along the coast or in mangrove backwaters, places where law enforcement patrols are scarce. Others suggest that offshore dumping of seized narcotics or even cargo ship losses could be a factor, though no direct evidence exists yet.

An environmental prosecutor in Santos, who asked to remain unnamed for security reasons, says investigations are underway: “We have reports of suspicious waste disposal in remote estuarine areas. If we prove illegal labs are dumping cocaine byproducts, there will be serious legal consequences.”

Cleanup poses its own challenges. Traditional wastewater treatment doesn’t easily break down complex organic molecules like cocaine. Specialized filtration, advanced oxidation processes, or constructed wetlands might be necessary to remove these contaminants before they reach marine habitats. But implementing such solutions requires investment and cooperation between environmental agencies, health departments, and law enforcement.

**Piecemeal progress**

Meanwhile, the research team continues to refine their analyses, comparing samples from different seasons and locations to see if contamination spikes after heavy rainfall or near known smuggling routes. They hope that by understanding the timing and geography of contamination, they can guide enforcement actions and environmental interventions more effectively.

“There’s no quick fix,” says Melo. “We’re dealing with clandestine activities and hidden pollution. But at least now we know something is off, and we can start asking the right questions.”

As for the sharks themselves, the next steps include monitoring their health indicators—growth rates, reproductive success, stress hormones—and seeing if these correlate with pollutant levels. If the sharks begin showing subtle declines, it may confirm that these contaminants are more than just chemical curiosities; they’re environmental threats demanding urgent attention.

No one expected to find traces of hard drugs in small coastal sharks. But as these Brazilian sharpnose sharks swim through coastal waters altered by human vice and negligence, they carry silent testimony to what lies upstream—and the complex web of consequences that follow.

"It’s not something I’d talk about with my neighbors, but after the storm, I swear I heard voices in that empty house next door," says Roland Perez, a resident of Port Arthur, Texas, describing a strange experience a few months after Hurricane Harvey in 2017. The structure he’s referring to had been condemned following catastrophic flooding, its walls streaked with mold and its beams cracked from high winds. Perez doesn’t believe in the supernatural—at least he didn’t until he stood in knee-deep water by a ruined front porch and thought he saw a faint figure drifting through a half-collapsed hallway.

**Disasters and Unsettled Ground**  
In the aftermath of hurricanes, tsunamis, floods, and earthquakes, rumors of ghosts or strange apparitions often surge through the affected communities. This pattern isn’t new. After the Great Kanto earthquake in Japan a century ago, local folklore emerged with stories of wandering spirits in devastated neighborhoods. More recently, after Hurricane Katrina in New Orleans, some residents started reporting ghostly sightings in abandoned homes and waterlogged cemeteries.

What’s behind these claims? According to Dr. Marisol Varela, a cultural anthropologist at the University of Louisiana at Lafayette, traumatic events reshape community narratives. "When entire blocks are destroyed, the familiar landmarks vanish," she says. "People are left with the emotional residue of loss—family members who didn’t survive, neighbors who moved away, entire histories washed out to sea. That lingering grief can manifest as tales of the unexplained."

**Psychological Fallout**  
On a psychological level, disasters create fertile ground for the human mind to interpret odd sounds or fleeting shadows as something otherworldly. Disrupted sleep cycles, heightened anxiety, and grief-induced hallucinations can lead to sensations that feel paranormal. "It’s well-documented that extreme stress and trauma can alter perception," says Dr. Hector Ramirez, a psychologist at Tulane University’s School of Public Health and Tropical Medicine. "In devastated neighborhoods, survivors sometimes suffer from acute stress disorders. The brain, seeking coherence in chaos, may turn creaking beams and distant groans of shifting debris into voices or apparitions."

Such phenomena have parallels in wartime environments, where soldiers, exhausted and sleep-deprived, report phantom footsteps or whispered commands. The principle is similar: in extreme conditions, the mind tries to construct patterns out of random stimuli, sometimes producing eerie illusions.

**Invisible Hazards Underfoot**  
But there may be more tangible reasons behind these "hauntings" as well. In the wreckage left by storms, floods, and earthquakes, buildings can release toxic fumes. When drywall crumbles, paint flakes off, and old insulation comes loose, chemicals like formaldehyde or asbestos can enter the air. "Exposure to certain toxins, especially in poorly ventilated spaces, can cause dizziness, confusion, and even mild hallucinations," says Dr. Leah Fischer, an environmental health researcher at the University of Texas Medical Branch in Galveston. "If someone ventures into a half-collapsed home trying to salvage belongings, they might feel lightheaded or see things that aren’t there."

This link between chemical exposure and strange sensations adds a practical dimension to what some might dismiss as superstition. Following the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami in Japan, several studies pointed to indoor contaminants—lead dust, mold spores, volatile organic compounds—released into the environment. Some local health officials recorded spikes in reports of dizziness and visual disturbances. While these were never formally categorized as "ghost sightings," the symptoms overlap with what could be interpreted as paranormal encounters if taken out of context.

**Shared Stories, Reinforcing Belief**  
Paranormal rumors thrive in social ecosystems hit hard by tragedy. In communities where electricity is patchy, streets are deserted at dusk, and nature’s silence is interrupted only by the drip of stagnant water, neighbors sometimes exchange uncanny anecdotes. "It’s not about believing in ghosts from the start," Varela says. "It’s about making sense of an environment that suddenly feels wrong. If one person says they saw a figure in the old pharmacy building, others may become more attuned to odd sounds, amplifying the cycle."

Local media can inadvertently feed this feedback loop. Headlines about haunted shelters or strange lights flickering in abandoned apartment blocks provide a narrative hook. In New Orleans post-Katrina, several ghost tour operators began including damaged districts in their routes. While many guides focused on documented history, a few leaned into rumor, further embedding the notion that spirits roamed these blasted landscapes.

**Cultural Layers and Interpretations**  
Cultural background also influences how people interpret the unexplainable. After Cyclone Nargis devastated Myanmar in 2008, accounts of restless spirits emerged from Buddhist monks who saw the dead as souls trapped in a transitional state. In Haitian communities, where vodou traditions are deeply ingrained, natural disasters sometimes trigger beliefs that restless lwa (spirits) have stirred, their influence made visible in collapsed temples and ruined marketplaces.

These cultural frames don’t just promote belief in ghosts; they offer comfort or a structured way to understand suffering. "A shared story of a ghost may help people bond, vent sorrow, or express anger at the slow pace of recovery efforts," says Ramirez. "It’s not always about literal belief. Sometimes it’s about finding meaning where there is only rubble."

**No Single Explanation**  
It’s tempting to file these tales under folklore or gullibility, but experts caution against simple explanations. After all, disaster zones challenge every aspect of human life—from basic health and safety to the realm of faith and imagination. Chemical exposures, psychological stress, cultural narratives, and social bonding all mix together in these shaken worlds.

As for Perez in Port Arthur, he never did find out what caused the strange vision. He still doesn’t call himself a believer in ghosts, but he no longer dismisses neighbors who claim they’ve "seen something" drifting through empty homes. "When you’ve lost everything," he says, "it’s not so easy to tell what’s real and what’s just your mind trying to fill in the blanks."
title: Why more natural disasters could trigger a rise in paranormal beliefs

A young saber-toothed cat, no bigger than a medium-sized house pet, has emerged from Siberia’s permafrost so intact that its stubby whiskers, downy fur, and even the folds around its paw pads remain visible. Local reindeer herders discovered the frozen cub last August along a riverbank in Yakutia, a region already famous for yielding the remains of woolly mammoths and extinct bison. But this is the first time researchers have seen a saber-toothed cat preserved with such incredible detail. The cub’s species, likely a type of Homotherium—an extinct genus known from scattered fossils—roamed Eurasia over 20,000 years ago, stalking steppe bison and horses under unforgiving Ice Age skies.

Unlike typical fossilized bones pried from rock layers, this cub is a natural freeze-dried mummy: its skin, muscles, stomach contents, and even internal organs appear astonishingly intact. “We’ve had fragments and partial skeletons of saber-toothed cats from across the Northern Hemisphere,” says Dr. Albert Protopopov, head of the mammoth fauna studies department at the Academy of Sciences in Yakutsk. “But nothing comes close to this. It’s as though we’ve met the animal only yesterday.”

**Preservation in the permafrost**  
The cub, estimated to be just a few months old at death, likely ended up entombed after tumbling into a natural trap—perhaps a small ravine or a concealed hole. Once buried, it remained in permafrost that never fully thawed, even during interglacial warm spells. The region, located along the remote Tirekhtyakh River, has previously yielded cave lion cubs and a young woolly rhino, but never a saber-toothed cat. The discovery underscores just how vast and relatively unexplored these northern deposits remain.

“When I saw the first photographs sent by the local finders, I had to catch my breath,” says Dr. Love Dalén, an evolutionary geneticist at the Centre for Palaeogenetics in Stockholm, who has collaborated on similar permafrost discoveries. “We have cave lion cubs from this region, but a Homotherium kitten is next-level rare. It’s a bridge straight into the past, unfiltered by the usual decay.”

**Hunting habits and anatomy**  
Saber-toothed cats—which included several genera, the most famous being North and South American Smilodon—were top predators that took down large herbivores. But in Eurasia, Homotherium was a different beast from its American cousins: built for endurance rather than brute strength, with somewhat shorter upper canines that curved elegantly. This mummy may confirm theories about Homotherium’s body proportions, coat patterns, and even how its baby teeth erupted compared to modern big cats.

Without traditional fur patterns or living relatives, no one is entirely certain what color these cats were. Many artists paint them as tawny or patched with stripes. Now scientists can examine the cub’s coat under the microscope and apply mass spectrometry to tease out pigments. “If we recover original melanin molecules,” says Dr. Edana Lord, a molecular biologist specializing in ancient DNA at Stockholm University, “we could say something about its coat color—dark, light, maybe even banded with subtle markings. That’s the kind of detail we rarely get from fossils.”

**Genetic insights**  
Because the cub’s soft tissues are intact, the team expects to retrieve high-quality genetic material. Genetic sequencing can yield far more than a family tree: it might hint at adaptations for hunting in low-light conditions, tolerance of frigid climates, or metabolic quirks that helped the species survive in an ecosystem dominated by mammoths, woolly rhinoceroses, and giant deer.

“For a start, we want to confirm it’s a Homotherium,” says Protopopov. “We assume that from skull morphology and tooth shape, but genetics will settle it. Then we can see how closely related it is to Homotherium populations known from central Europe or Alaska. Were there distinct lineages roaming these steppes, or did they form one large population?”

Moreover, stable isotope analysis of the cub’s tissues might reveal what its mother ate, since nursing offspring often carry chemical signatures inherited from maternal milk. By comparing these isotopes with known prey species from the region, scientists can narrow down the menu of a saber-toothed cat family. “If we find that its mother’s diet leaned heavily on young horses, that’s one clue to hunting strategy,” says Dalén. “If, on the other hand, reindeer or muskox dominated, that suggests different prey selection.”

**Beyond basic biology**  
This mummy also hints at social behaviors. Did Homotherium mothers stash their cubs in dens? Were they solitary or did they hunt cooperatively, like modern lions? The cub’s find spot—far from deep caves—suggests it might have been sheltered in some above-ground hideout, possibly under shrubs or in a small depression. One can imagine a mother cat leaving her offspring briefly while she pursued prey, only to never return. But until more individuals turn up, it’s hard to be certain.

“We’re piecing together a puzzle from just one fragment,” says Dr. Yukiko Tatsuro, a paleontologist at Hokkaido University who has worked on cave lion cubs but not involved in this study. “But even one well-preserved cub can test or refine existing assumptions. Maybe Homotherium was less cave-oriented, or maybe they used a wider range of habitats than we once thought.”

**Darker realities and cultural interest**  
While the scientific value is enormous, there’s a quiet undercurrent of loss. The cub’s species—and the entire Pleistocene megafauna—disappeared thousands of years ago, influenced by shifting climates and possibly human activity. Now, as permafrost warms due to climate change, more such remains may surface. This offers unprecedented opportunities, but it also exposes delicate finds to decay and looting. Local communities, scientists, and regional authorities must balance curiosity with conservation.

The mummy will likely reside in a specialized cold-storage facility at the Academy of Sciences in Yakutsk, where experts will X-ray its skeletal structure and carry out careful dissections of tiny tissue samples. Tourists and students might eventually see it on display once initial research concludes. Already, field rumors have sparked excitement. Social media chatter in Yakutsk’s small cafés, where paleontologists sometimes gather after long days in cold labs, bubbles with speculation: Will we be able to see the spots on its fur, read its last meal from its intestines, or even reconstruct its DNA?

**No neat final word**  
There’s no final verdict yet—just a flurry of tests and waiting for data. Scientists will be cautious. Each step is painstaking: a small snippet of ear tissue to test for pigments, a tiny bone sample for isotopes. Every result will stir debate, spark new hypotheses. The cub, silent and still after so many millennia, now speaks volumes through its preserved flesh.

Protopopov puts it plainly: “We’re suddenly face-to-face with an ancient predator that lived in a world we barely understand. I expect it will keep us busy for years, maybe decades.”

Many assume lipstick’s global popularity took off in recent centuries, but humans were staining their lips bright red thousands of years ago. Early inhabitants of Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley mixed crushed gemstones or red iron oxides with fats to create rudimentary lip paints. Cleopatra, famously, is said to have brewed her scarlet hue by blending carmine beetles and ants—an elaborate process that produced a color as coveted as any prized gem in her court.

Yet from the start, red lips carried meaning that stretched beyond simple adornment. In ancient Greece, brothel workers were legally required to wear red lip color, distinguishing them from “respectable” women. “Prostitutes’ red lips served as a kind of calling card,” says Lisa Eldridge, a makeup historian and author of *Face Paint: The Story of Makeup.* “In that context, paint on the mouth wasn’t just decorative—it was a deliberate, highly visible signal.” The pigment and sheen made their presence clear in Athenian markets and alleyways, fostering a link between scarlet lips and sensual allure that still echoes today.

As new trade networks emerged in the Mediterranean, potions for coloring the lips traveled widely, shifting recipes from plant-based pigments to ingredients like cochineal insects imported from the Americas. In medieval Europe, however, the pendulum swung dramatically. The Christian Church condemned any pigment that seemed to alter one’s “God-given” face. A woman brazen enough to sport crimson lips risked accusations of sorcery. Some theologians called red lips “Satan’s snares,” and in the British Isles, rumors spread that witches charmed their victims by bewitching their lip ointments. It was a precarious time to flaunt a carmine pout.

Despite these dangers, certain aristocrats and royal figures continued to admire painted lips behind closed doors. Queen Elizabeth I, known for her stark white face paint, famously highlighted her mouth with vermilion. In the early modern period, Venice’s courtesans dared to echo the vivid hues that had once branded their Greek counterparts. Eventually, by the 17th and 18th centuries, red lipstick filtered into high society. French nobles dabbled in lip rouge, and Italian perfumeries sold tinted balms. But the stigma lingered. In 1770, Britain’s Parliament debated legislation that would have allowed men to annul marriages if wives had “seduced” them by using makeup—especially lip rouge.

The last time 63-year-old Jeff Russell visited Watoga State Park, he was stunned by how silent and shadowy the forest seemed after dark. He’d brought his teenage granddaughter along, hoping to show her the kind of nighttime he remembered as a boy—back before porch lamps, parking lot floodlights, and billboard glows had carved into every corner of the landscape. “I wanted her to realize that we humans didn’t always flood the world with light,” he says, recalling that drive into a part of West Virginia where the state park’s rangers had worked for decades to keep electrical illumination to a bare minimum.

The result? Watoga’s nights aren’t just dark; they’re downright inky. Here, the sky spills with stars, and on summer evenings, the real spectacle begins along the quiet trails and dimly lit park roads: thousands of synchronous fireflies rise from the leaf litter and pulse in perfect harmony. In a clearing near Monongaseneka Overlook, you can stand motionless and watch their flickering dance sweep across the understory in silent waves.

While fireflies blink worldwide, synchronous fireflies—species that flash in coordinated bursts—remain rare. Places like Great Smoky Mountains National Park have drawn crowds for years, but Watoga only gained notice more recently. That’s partly because visitors and rangers protected the park’s natural darkness without even knowing what lived there. “We never intended to create a stage for fireflies,” says Kelly Raines, a Watoga ranger who’s been with the park for over 25 years. “We were just trying to respect the habitat and keep an authentic night sky. The fireflies were a gift we discovered along the way.”

**The Fight Against Light**  
When the park first opened in the 1930s, the surrounding counties still relied mostly on lanterns and moonlight. Over time, artificial lighting crept closer. By the early 2000s, however, the park’s leadership made a decision: all new lighting would be shielded, and any unnecessary outdoor illumination would be removed. This policy wasn’t widely advertised, nor did they call it “dark-sky stewardship” at the time. They just didn’t want to waste electricity or distract campers from the stars.

Rangers replaced standard bulbs in visitor areas with lower-wattage lights and installed covers to focus beams downward. Maintenance crews tallied the lights in parking lots and restrooms, cutting excess fixtures. Park neighbors—family farms, small homesteads, and a scattering of cabins—were encouraged to follow suit. Within a few years, Watoga’s nightscape had grown remarkably shadowy for an eastern U.S. destination. The decision was practical, but it had an unexpected ecological payoff: more fireflies.

Artificial lights disrupt fireflies, often preventing them from finding mates. Dr. Michael J. Raupp, an entomologist at the University of Maryland, explains, “Fireflies flash patterns to communicate—males signal from the air, females respond from the ground. Ambient light pollution can scramble these signals, making courtship difficult or impossible.” By keeping things dark, Watoga offered these beetles prime conditions to thrive.

**Surprised by Sparkles**  
It wasn’t until about a decade ago that longtime campers started reporting something peculiar: a population of fireflies that didn’t just blink at random, but seemed to coordinate their glows. “At first I thought it was a trick of my eyes,” says Brenda King, who’s camped at Watoga every summer since 2010. “But I’d be out in a meadow at dusk, and the flashes would come in waves—on, off, on, off. It looked like a Christmas display out there.”

As word spread, a small number of entomologists and nature photographers arrived to confirm the reports. Synchronous fireflies, known scientifically in the U.S. as Photinus carolinus, have a stronghold in the Smokies, but sightings in West Virginia were scarce until now. On several evenings in late June, researchers from West Virginia University and volunteers from a local naturalist club documented large clusters of these fireflies performing their signature chorus of flickering. Their findings suggest Watoga may hold one of the northernmost known populations of synchronous fireflies in the Appalachian region.

Laura Mann, a researcher assisting with the count, recalls her first night knee-deep in ferns, notebook in hand: “I’d seen photos of synchronous fireflies before, but witnessing it in person was something else. When a thousand tiny lanterns blink on and off together, it’s mesmerizing. You can’t help but gasp.”

**Life in the Glow**  
For the fireflies, coordination improves their chances of successful mating. When males blink in sync, females may respond more readily, ensuring that the next generation of larvae will soon be burrowing into the leaf mold. Down the line, that means more fireflies—and a cycle that supports healthier populations in a time when insects everywhere face threats from pesticides and habitat loss.

Park officials now see the fireflies as a valuable asset—yet they’re cautious. “The last thing we want is to draw massive crowds and risk disturbing them,” says Raines. Instead, they’re quietly sharing best practices with visitors: use red-light flashlights, avoid trampling vegetation, keep quiet, and give the insects space to perform. There are no official firefly-viewing festivals here—just a hint from a ranger, or a whisper passed at a campsite picnic table.

Back on that breezy, star-flooded night, Russell’s granddaughter—who’d grown up with brightly lit streets—asked him why they didn’t just bring a flashlight or turn on their car’s headlights to see better. He shook his head. “If we did that, we might miss what’s unfolding all around us,” he told her, nodding toward the softly glowing spectacle in the forest. In the hush and the gloom of Watoga, nature’s light show is all you need to guide the way.
title: Fireflies are nature’s light show at this West Virginia state park

David Mayer, who died in 2013, had been a professor at a small liberal arts college in upstate New York, teaching philosophy and ethics. According to several colleagues and former students interviewed by phone, he was relatively unknown outside his field, the author of a few journal articles on metaphysics, and active in local community groups. He wasn’t a celebrity, nor the subject of any known scandals. Yet, the chatbot’s refusal to utter his name sparked a minor online uproar and raised a bigger question: How exactly do these A.I. models decide which content to block, and why?

If certain phrases or categories of information appear on internal “do not say” lists—or if the model’s training data suggests that discussing a name might involve personal details that run afoul of privacy policies—the AI may block itself from mentioning it altogether. “It’s a reminder that these filters are sometimes clumsy,” said Dr. Marianne Yates, an associate professor at Carnegie Mellon University who studies algorithmic bias and data curation. “They’re supposed to protect people from harmful or private information, but they can also misfire, flagging something harmless.” Dr. Yates emphasized that as more chatbots come online, users may encounter more instances where an AI’s privacy rules collide with perfectly normal requests.

Squirting cucumbers are not exactly garden celebrities, but these spiky, olive-sized fruits pack a startling defense system: when ripe, they launch their seeds with enough force to startle an unsuspecting passer-by. According to new research, these botanical grenadiers can fling their tiny projectiles nearly 40 feet through the air. And while this phenomenon has been documented by naturalists for centuries, the precise mechanics have remained murky—until now.

The plant at the heart of this high-pressure drama is the squirting cucumber (*Ecballium elaterium*), a species native to the Mediterranean region. It produces small, knobby fruits that, at a glance, look like miniature water balloons draped in fine hairs. But inside each fruit, fluid pressure builds steadily as it matures. At a certain point, the slightest disturbance—such as an animal brushing past or a light gust of wind—causes the fruit to detach from its stem, suddenly releasing an interior slurry of seeds and pulp.

“People have known about squirting cucumbers for centuries,” said Dr. Paolo Ricci, a plant physiologist at the University of Padua in Italy who has studied Mediterranean flora for over a decade. “They appear in old herbal manuscripts, with descriptions of the seeds shooting out like tiny arrows. Yet how they generate such a remarkable force has puzzled botanists.”

In a study published this month in the journal *Interface*, a team of scientists set out to decode the physics behind this explosive seed dispersal. Using high-speed cameras, pressure sensors, and fresh samples grown in test plots near Athens, they recorded the fruits at the exact moment they snapped off their stems. By slowing the footage down to a few thousand frames per second, the researchers observed how the fruit’s internal pressure, built up over days, was channeled into a split-second release.

The key, they found, lies in the cucumber’s internal architecture. Each fruit is essentially a fluid-filled capsule with a thicker rind at the stem end. As water and dissolved sugars accumulate inside, the internal pressure can climb to several times normal atmospheric pressure. This tension is kept in check until a small “weak point” around the stem finally fails. Once that point ruptures, the fruit transforms into a natural water cannon, ejecting seeds at speeds that can top 30 feet per second.

“Think of it like twisting a balloon full of water,” said Dr. Natalia Sideris, an applied biomechanist at the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens and an author of the study. “There’s a moment when the force inside just overwhelms the balloon’s skin. With the squirting cucumber, the fruit’s structure and fluid content create this perfect storm of pressure. The instant the stem seals break, everything inside blasts outward.”

The seeds, surrounded by a slimy gel, are propelled far from the parent plant. This is a critical evolutionary advantage: by flinging its offspring across a wide area, the squirting cucumber reduces competition among seedlings and increases the odds that some will sprout in favorable conditions. The mechanism is a vivid example of how plants, despite their sedentary nature, have evolved ingenious strategies to spread their genes.

One surprising revelation came from measuring the angles and trajectories of the seeds. The team found that the fruit’s internal geometry helps direct the seeds in a roughly horizontal spread, not just randomly upward or downward. “We saw this consistent radial pattern,” said Dr. Sideris. “It’s not just an explosion—it’s a controlled blast that maximizes seed distribution.”

The researchers believe that understanding such natural dispersal methods might offer insights into engineering applications—perhaps in designing small-scale devices that harness fluid pressure for precise projectile launches. It’s not the first time botanists have inspired inventors; burrs led to Velcro, and lotus leaves inspired water-repellent coatings. Now, the squirting cucumber may claim a small place in the pantheon of nature’s design innovations.

Still, Dr. Ricci cautions that this research is motivated by curiosity, not commerce. “To me, it’s about appreciating the sheer cleverness of plant evolution,” he said. “We tend to think of plants as passive, but here’s one that’s rigged to go off like a tiny catapult. If you’ve ever doubted the dynamism of the plant kingdom, a face full of cucumber seeds might change your mind.” Without a neat narrative arc or any polite warnings, the squirting cucumber simply does its thing—quietly biding its time until it’s ready to fire.

Grizzly Bear 399, one of the most watched and photographed animals in the Yellowstone region, was struck and killed by a vehicle last week along a highway just south of Grand Teton National Park. She was 28, an age that few wild grizzlies reach, and had raised 18 cubs over her lifetime, earning the affectionate moniker of “supermom” among wildlife enthusiasts, park staff, and generations of returning visitors.

Wildlife authorities reported that the collision occurred at dusk on U.S. Highway 89, near the Pilgrim Creek drainage, an area she often roamed while foraging for berries and fishing for cutthroat trout. It’s not unusual for grizzlies to cross roadways in that region, where protected lands border working ranches and scenic byways. In this case, rangers said the vehicle’s driver notified authorities and stayed on the scene. The driver’s identity has not been released, and investigators have not announced any charges.

Grizzly 399’s rise to local stardom began more than a decade ago. Her home range spanned parts of Grand Teton National Park and surrounding national forests, as well as occasional forays near Yellowstone’s southern boundary. In contrast to most grizzlies, which tend to shy away from roads and people, she often raised her cubs in areas visible from public pullouts, allowing nature lovers to observe them from a safe distance. Photographers from as far as Tokyo and Berlin camped out at dawn, hoping for a fleeting shot of her leading a brood of fluffy cubs over a meadow.

“She gave visitors something astonishing: the chance to see a wild grizzly being a grizzly, not just once in a lifetime, but year after year,” said Taylor Wilcox, a local wildlife guide who has led tours in the Jackson Hole area for nearly 20 years. “People planned entire trips around the possibility of spotting 399 and her cubs. She became woven into the experience of traveling here, like Old Faithful or the Snake River Overlook.”

Several cafes and gear shops in Jackson Hole prominently displayed photos of 399, and at least one coffee shop offered a “Bear 399 Latte”—a hazelnut mocha that regulars claim is named for the bear’s rich, dark coat and the sweet surprises she brought to visitors’ days. Social media pages dedicated to the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem frequently featured updates on which drainage she might be roaming or how many cubs she was leading that season.

For wildlife managers, her fame was a mixed blessing. On one hand, her presence offered a strong reminder of successful conservation efforts: The region’s grizzly population has rebounded from perilously low numbers in the mid-20th century. On the other, it raised difficult questions about habituation, traffic risks, and what it means when wild creatures draw crowds.

Park officials repeatedly issued guidelines: Never approach her or her cubs, keep a minimum viewing distance of 100 yards, store food securely, and never block the road to gawk. Despite the excitement she inspired, rangers stressed the need to remember that she was not tame, and the region’s highways were never intended as wildlife viewing platforms.

“She knew how to navigate these landscapes, but the margins of safety can be razor-thin,” said Wyatt Krause, a biologist with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. “A bear is an expert in finding ripened berries or digging out ground squirrels, but they don’t understand the concept of oncoming traffic. Collisions happen, even when drivers aren’t acting recklessly.”

Krause noted that accidents involving wildlife are not uncommon in the Greater Yellowstone area. Ungulates like elk and mule deer are often hit during migration season, and even smaller animals like porcupines turn up as roadside casualties. But the death of Bear 399 will likely resonate more deeply. She was, in a sense, an ambassador for her species. Her ability to raise multiple sets of cubs—18 in total—made her family line a focus of field studies on grizzly reproduction and longevity.

Local naturalists recall that she was first collared as a young adult, allowing biologists to track her movements and better understand how adult females pass along key survival skills to their offspring. Many of her cubs have gone on to establish their own territories. Some are still in the region, meaning that her genetic legacy will likely continue to shape local grizzly behavior for years.

“I remember watching her teaching her cubs how to forage in a patch of huckleberry shrubs near Willow Flats,” said Jessica Lang, a wildlife photographer based in Bozeman, Mont., who has followed the bear since 2010. “Seeing them tumble over each other, learning what to eat, how to interact with the world—it was like watching a tiny kingdom under her guidance. Each time I return, I look at the meadows and the streams and think, ‘She lived right here, and her family still roams.’

In death, Grizzly 399 may end up a reminder of what it takes to share wild spaces with large predators. Visitors and residents continue to speak of her in present tense—out of habit, or perhaps out of a wish to hold onto her presence just a bit longer. Traffic continues to flow along those roads, and other bears still wander those valleys. But for those who tracked her story, the absence of that towering, wise old matriarch will not soon be forgotten.

The head of the Roman emperor Septimius Severus, a prized bronze fragment held for decades at Copenhagen’s Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek, is on its way back to Turkey. In a move that reflects growing scrutiny over the origins of ancient artifacts in European collections, the Danish museum agreed to return the sculpture’s head after concluding it was most likely looted from a Roman-era shrine in southwestern Turkey.

**Rediscovering a Troubled Provenance**  
Septimius Severus, who ruled from A.D. 193 to 211, was a North African–born leader celebrated for shoring up Roman frontiers and consolidating imperial power. Statues of emperors were commonly displayed in civic and religious settings across the empire, including in wealthy Anatolian towns. Scholars say the head now destined for return once adorned a life-size statue in the Roman city of Bubon, an ancient Lycian settlement located in what is now Burdur Province.

He doesn’t charge a dime, and he never asks for anything in return. For the past two years, a small wooden shed behind a modest duplex in Silver Spring, Maryland, has quietly kept dozens of people rolling around town on bicycles—no strings attached. On a typical weekend afternoon, you might catch Manuel Vera hunched over a dented frame, wiping down scuffed handlebars, or fishing loose spokes out of a bin. Sometimes he’s got three bikes lined up for repairs. Other times he’s got a couple dozen stacked precariously along the fence. Most of them, old Raleighs or battered Treks, were donated after neighbors spotted Manuel’s flyer at a local café or heard about him through the school grapevine.

Silver Spring has long drawn immigrants and refugees from Latin America, West Africa, Southeast Asia, and the Middle East, among many other places. The city’s location just north of Washington, D.C., has made it easier for families to resettle, find work, and gradually build new lives. But adjusting to a new country isn’t simple—especially when newcomers don’t have reliable transportation. That’s where Manuel’s free bike shed comes in.

Originally from El Salvador, Manuel settled here with his parents in the late ’90s. He still remembers arriving as a kid, not speaking much English, and feeling a bit trapped in their small apartment since his father often took the only family car to two different jobs. “I would’ve given anything for a bike,” Manuel recalls. “It would’ve made running errands or going to the park way less of a hassle.” He eventually saved up for a cheap secondhand bike as a teenager, and when he started working in construction after high school, he’d often ride it to job sites around town.

A few years back, Manuel noticed that some newly arrived families—people he met through St. Michael’s Parish and the Gilchrist Immigrant Resource Center—faced the same challenges he had. Transportation was always the first hurdle. He also noticed that local thrift shops rarely carried decent, affordable bikes. One day, he hauled a broken-down hybrid he’d found abandoned in a neighbor’s yard into his shed out back. After a little tinkering, he resurrected it with parts from a yard sale. He passed it along to a young man who had just arrived from Eritrea, and within a week, that man had found a better-paying job a few miles away. “He said it cut his commute down by more than half,” Manuel says. “I guess that’s when the lightbulb came on.”

Manuel began spreading the word. As neighbors and local teachers caught wind, they started showing up with old bikes collecting dust in their basements. Before long, he had a dozen bikes, then two dozen. Most needed new brake pads or fresh cables. Manuel learned how to fix them up by watching YouTube videos at night. He went through several weekends hunched over stubborn chains, occasionally shouting in frustration when a bolt refused to budge. He doesn’t claim to be a professional mechanic, but he’s gotten pretty good at cobbling together safe, reliable rides.

Local advocates say what he’s doing is more than a nice gesture. “A bike can mean everything to someone trying to establish a stable life,” explains Susan Menendez, a coordinator at the International Rescue Committee’s regional office in nearby Hyattsville. “When a family has access to wheels, they can reach English classes, job interviews, and the grocery store without relying on expensive taxis or bus transfers. It can be a real game-changer.”

On a cloudy Wednesday last spring, a single mother from Honduras, who asked to go only by Yolanda, picked up a refurbished mountain bike for her teenage daughter. The girl, who had been struggling to adjust at a new high school, rode that bike to meet a friend in another neighborhood for the very first time. “My daughter came home smiling. She said, ‘I feel free,’” Yolanda recalls. “It might sound silly, but a bike helps you feel like you belong here.”

Manuel shrugs off the praise. He jokes that he’s just clearing out junk. He’s still juggling his construction work and his own family life, so he doesn’t have grand plans for expansion, nor is he looking to start a formal charity. For now, he’ll keep puttering around in his shed out back, adjusting seat posts and changing flats, and seeing who else can use a lift.

Walk along St. Charles Avenue during Carnival season, and you’ll spot a series of towering floats with riders tossing beads and trinkets into the cheering crowd. You may also notice something else: every single person on those floats is masked. This isn’t just tradition—it’s actually required by city ordinance. For all the costumes, music, and king cakes floating around, the mask rule remains one of the few ironclad expectations placed on those who ride.

“Mardi Gras has long been about stepping outside everyday rules,” says Arthur Hardy, publisher of **Arthur Hardy’s Mardi Gras Guide**, who has chronicled the season for decades. “When riders hide their faces, it helps break down social barriers. It’s not about who you are back at the office or how much money you make. Everyone on that float is an equal participant in the fun.”

The masking custom dates back to the 19th century, when members of the earliest krewes—Rex, Proteus, Momus—sought ways to mingle with neighbors without being identified. Masking allowed a well-known judge to stand next to a dockworker without anyone gawking or drawing lines based on station. Today, city rules still demand that every float rider remain masked from start to finish. If you try to flout that requirement, you risk being removed before the parade even begins.

“Mardi Gras was born out of old European masquerade traditions,” explains Dr. Kim Vaz-Deville, a New Orleans scholar who has written extensively about the city’s carnival heritage. “Wearing a mask means you’re free to interact with folks you might never speak to otherwise. It’s one reason the season still feels so refreshing—it shuffles the deck.”

This sense of anonymity is part of what makes Mardi Gras different from other celebrations. In places like Rio de Janeiro or Venice, costumes might be dazzling, but the New Orleans approach makes face coverings a firm rule for those riding the floats. The city takes this seriously enough that officers have, on occasion, reminded krewes to check their riders’ masks before rolling.

Local riders take the custom in stride. “I’ve been on a float in the Krewe of Muses for more than 15 years,” says Sandra Martin, a participant who asked that her last name be used to help preserve her mystique. “I love that no one knows it’s me under there. It’s wild—I can throw beads to my boss or my own cousin, and they have no idea. It levels the field and keeps the spirit of surprise alive.”

The mask rule also helps maintain the carnival’s time-honored mystique. Without it, a parade might feel a bit like a corporate promo or a social club outing. Instead, you get something unpredictable, where everyone—from a local politician to a first-time visitor—stands side by side, catching beads from a stranger whose identity remains hidden behind bright feathers and sequins.

If you find yourself along the parade route, gazing up at the color and chaos, don’t expect to recognize the faces grinning behind those masks. That’s the point. Mardi Gras, at its best, has always invited people to shake off their usual roles and just have a blast—anonymously. The mask keeps that spirit breathing, year after year.

For over seven decades on the throne, Queen Elizabeth II held fast to the quiet routines that shaped her life behind palace walls. Among these habits was one she rarely discussed in public: writing in her personal diary. She maintained this practice for most of her life, jotting down day-to-day observations and reflections in a manner that close confidants described as measured, private, and utterly without flourish. While her diary entries have never been released to the public—and it’s likely they never will be—several royal historians believe that the Queen’s very last note to herself, penned on the evening before her passing at Balmoral Castle, was as spare and self-effacing as the woman herself.

Robert Hardman, author of *Queen of Our Times: The Life of Elizabeth II*, has examined countless documents and spoken to many individuals who worked at the periphery of the Queen’s private world. Though no one beyond a small circle has actually seen the final diary entry, he says those who were close to Her Majesty throughout her reign all agree on one point: her writing habits were unfailingly consistent. “She recorded the day’s events almost like a ship’s log,” Hardman says. “It was a summary rather than a narrative, more concerned with what needed to be noted down than with emotion or deep introspection.” He stresses that this approach remained unchanged even after she lost her beloved husband, Prince Philip, in 2021. “If anything, her style became even more economical over time,” Hardman adds.

This consistent approach suggests that her last private note, if examined today, would likely come across as almost startlingly simple. Ingrid Seward, editor-in-chief of *Majesty* magazine and author of several royal biographies, notes that the Queen had a way of distilling her role into a handful of straightforward sentiments. “Duty was never something she treated as a grand concept,” Seward says. “For her, it was simply what she did—like breathing. There was no reason to elaborate.” Seward believes that if we ever learn the precise wording of that final entry, it might be just a line or two acknowledging that day’s light engagements or remarking on the weather, followed by a brief acknowledgment of her ongoing responsibility to the Crown. “It would be almost anticlimactic,” she says, “yet also perfectly fitting for who she was.”

The Queen’s diaries, rumored to fill entire shelves in secure archives, remain locked away. Royal tradition holds that these personal writings are considered private property, not historical documents to be published for future generations. “They’re not a confessional, and they’re certainly not intended for public consumption,” explains historian Hugo Vickers, who has written extensively on the Royal Family. According to Vickers, the Queen’s habit of writing these entries late at night, often after returning from a day’s official duties, gave her a chance to keep track of events, meetings, and impressions without imposing interpretation or sentiment. “Those closest to her have said she rarely used adjectives,” he points out. “She preferred facts: where she went, who she met, what was discussed—little more.”

Given that the Queen’s health declined gently over her final months, it’s possible she knew these would be her closing pages. Yet experts agree that even this awareness wouldn’t have prompted her to break form. In the weeks before her death, she met with the new Prime Minister, Liz Truss, fulfilling a final constitutional duty with calm resolve. There were no dramatic public statements from the palace, no grand farewell speeches. As Vickers puts it, “If she knew the end was coming, I doubt she would have penned anything profound or poetic. She would have done what she always did: quietly acknowledge another day as monarch.”

A former palace staffer, who asked not to be named, recalls a conversation with a lady-in-waiting many years ago. “I was curious and asked if the Queen ever wrote anything emotional, especially after difficult times like the Aberfan disaster or the death of Diana,” the staffer says. “The lady-in-waiting shrugged and said, ‘She writes what happened. That is all.’” If that was the case in moments of national tragedy, it’s almost certain it would hold true during the final hours of her life.

In a world now accustomed to oversharing, where public figures often reveal personal struggles in great detail, the Queen’s approach was a stark contrast. Her last written reflection would not be a manifesto or a spiritual parting note. Instead, say those who know her habits best, it was likely a handful of words that simply recorded the day’s quiet rhythm, perhaps an understated nod to her duty that said everything by saying very little.

Crows don’t rely on flashy feathers or fancy footwork to impress. Instead, some of them show a knack for numbers—one that can measure up to the counting abilities of an average two-year-old. Recent experiments suggest that these birds can size up small quantities and respond in a way that looks a lot like simple counting.

Andreas Nieder, a neurobiologist at the University of Tübingen in Germany, has spent years investigating the cognitive abilities of crows. His lab uses carefully designed tests to see how well these dark-plumed corvids distinguish between sets of dots or sounds. “We present them with a series of images, each containing a certain number of elements,” Nieder says. “Then we measure their responses to see if they recognize when two sets have the same count.”

It might sound like a carnival trick, but the crows’ numeric sensitivities have been confirmed under rigorous lab conditions. Researchers slide a crow into a quiet booth where it can peck at a touch screen. The animal sees two sets of shapes—maybe four triangles on one side and four circles on the other. If it picks the side that matches a previously shown target number, it receives a reward, such as a bit of chicken feed. After enough training, the crow makes the right choice at rates far above random guessing.

These findings have led some scientists to compare crow counting skills to those of human toddlers who can distinguish between small sets of objects before learning to count verbally. An 18-month-old child can often tell when three cookies differ from two. They may not say “three” out loud, but they know something changed. Crows seem to have a similar handle on small quantities, even though they never learn language or attend preschool. “It’s not about reciting numbers or doing arithmetic, of course,” Nieder says. “It’s more about recognizing that one set is bigger or smaller, or that two sets match in number.”

Interestingly, crows are not the only animals that show these abilities. Ravens, parrots, and even honeybees have demonstrated some level of numeric competence. Nonhuman primates can do it as well, though researchers suspect the underlying neural processes differ between species. Yet what stands out about crows is their apparent willingness to handle these tasks without much fuss. Even under conditions where no spoken commands are given, they keep picking the correct set.

To get a better grasp on the biological roots of this skill, Nieder’s team recorded activity from individual crow neurons. They found nerve cells in a part of the crow’s brain—akin to our association cortex—that fire in patterns corresponding to certain counts. A few neurons might light up when the crow sees two dots, and a different set of neurons might activate for three. These patterns appear whether the objects are large or small, bright or faint. The result is a brain that can code quantity abstractly, without relying on the exact shape or color of what it’s counting.

Cognitive scientists who focus on child development find these parallels intriguing. “If you show toddlers a few objects and then show them a second set with one more or one less, they tend to look longer at the changed number,” says Lisa Feigenson, a developmental psychologist at Johns Hopkins University who studies infant cognition. “They haven’t learned counting words yet, but they know that something is off.” Feigenson stresses that this is a rough similarity, not an equality. Toddlers also rely on language cues as they grow older, eventually mapping words like “one,” “two,” and “three” onto the concepts they’ve already intuited. Crows, of course, never take that linguistic leap—yet they can still handle comparisons that mimic what a pre-verbal child might do.

It’s still unclear why crows developed this numeric knack, though it may help them assess food sources or keep track of flock members. If a crow lands on a tree and spots three other crows, it might somehow sense that one is missing if only two fly away. Or perhaps it uses such mental tallying while pecking through a certain number of seeds scattered on the ground. The evolutionary details remain murky.

Even without a full explanation, the findings hint that number sense does not hinge on language. Crows cannot say “caw, caw, caw, caw” to label “four,” yet they seem to know when the amount before their eyes matches what they just saw. It’s as if deep inside their ebony feathers, these birds harbor a quiet, unspoken math that rivals the first steps of human counting.
