A clay tag no bigger than a thumb, pulled from a cramped stone grave in northern Syria, may rewrite the story of how humans recorded their words. Unlike the pictorial hieroglyphs of ancient Egypt or the wedge-shaped cuneiform imprints common throughout Mesopotamia, the markings on this tiny cylinder look suspiciously like individual letters. If confirmed, the find could be the earliest known example of an alphabetic script—one that relied on a limited set of symbols to represent spoken sounds—instead of the elaborate sign systems that came before.

The battered artifact, unearthed at a site near the Euphrates River by a team from the University of Tübingen, has been tentatively dated to around 2000 BCE. The tomb it came from contained the remains of at least three individuals and a handful of everyday goods, including pottery vessels and a small copper blade. What makes the clay tag stand out is that it appears to have been attached to a woven container—perhaps a gift or an offering left with the dead—and it bears roughly a dozen small signs incised in fresh clay before firing.

“This isn’t a big flashy tablet,” said Dr. Omar Amin, an archaeologist on the team. “It’s a modest object, basically a label that you’d tie onto a package. But it’s inscribed in a manner that doesn’t match hieroglyphs or cuneiform. Each symbol seems to represent a distinct sound. If that’s right, we’re looking at a very early alphabet, predating examples known from the Levant and the Sinai.”

The oldest recognized alphabets previously identified, such as those from ancient Semitic inscriptions in the southern Levant, date to roughly 1800 BCE. This new piece, if confirmed, would push back that timeline by a century or more, and place the invention of true alphabetic writing a good distance farther north. Amin said his team used a combination of digital microphotography and laser scanning (with a Leica confocal microscope borrowed from a materials lab) to study the depth and order of the strokes. “We can see that the scribe pressed and dragged a reed stylus in a careful sequence,” Amin said. “They weren’t sketching pictures—they were writing sounds.”

Not everyone is convinced. Dr. Layla Kattan, a specialist in Bronze Age scripts at the University of Chicago’s Oriental Institute, said it’s too early to declare victory. “It’s a compelling artifact, but the sample is tiny, and we don’t yet know what language it represents or whether it’s truly a full alphabet rather than some shorthand. We must find related examples at the site to build a stronger case,” she said.

Still, a few signs point toward it representing a known tongue. Amin said preliminary comparisons suggest the signs could encode a Northwest Semitic language, related to those later written in alphabets along the eastern Mediterranean. “We might be seeing the earliest steps toward a writing system that inspired countless others,” he said. “We’re working to locate more fragments or tablets in the surrounding strata. If we can show similar inscriptions, we’ll have a better chance of decoding this.”

For now, the clay tag’s meaning remains opaque. Some signs look like simplified versions of animal heads or tools, but no one can say what they stood for. The team plans to conduct chemical analysis of sediment still clinging to the tag’s surface, hoping to identify traces of organic fibers that might confirm it was tied onto a basket or cloth pouch. Until more evidence emerges, this tiny bit of clay will sit in a lab drawer—quiet but full of tantalizing promise—waiting for someone to sound out its silent marks.

Late last year, a team of materials scientists at the University of Manchester developed a peculiar window dressing: a thin silk curtain embedded with a special vibrating fiber. This textile can hush the roar of traffic, blaring car horns, and even construction racket. By mimicking the way noise-canceling headphones produce a counter-signal to unwanted sounds, the new curtain cuts through city clamor without relying on bulky insulation panels or thick double glazing.

**From Headphones to Windows**  
Standard noise barriers—heavy foam walls, sealed triple-pane windows—often weigh a ton and can turn homes into airless bunkers. The Manchester group, led by materials researcher Sarah Roth, wanted a simpler approach. Roth’s team took inspiration from everyday headphones that quiet a subway commute by producing an out-of-phase hum to counteract external noise. That basic idea—using vibrations to interfere with incoming sound waves—spurred their design of a textile that could hang in an ordinary window frame.

They started with raw silk because it’s strong, flexible, and easy to stitch with unusual threads. Into this fabric, they sewed a slender conductive fiber containing piezoelectric elements—tiny bits of material that flex when jolted by an electrical signal. When the fiber “hears” incoming noise through a small attached sensor (essentially a microphone sewn along the curtain’s edge), it’s driven to vibrate at frequencies that cancel some of the sound. Unlike big window replacements or clunky external shutters, this shimmering textile is barely a millimeter thick, allowing natural light in and leaving the view unobscured.

“We’ve always known that sound is just pressure waves,” says Roth, sitting in her cramped workshop at the University of Manchester’s Sackville Street Building. “If we can produce a wave pattern that opposes the incoming pressure fluctuations, we can reduce what a listener actually hears.” Roth’s team tested a prototype in a lab chamber simulating noise from a busy street: during peak screeches, measured sound levels dropped by about 12 decibels after passing through the energized curtain. That difference won’t render a roadway whisper-quiet, but it can make a noticeable dent in the irritation factor.

**Why Silk Makes Sense**  
Silk’s role here isn’t just aesthetic. According to co-author Li Wei, who specializes in textile engineering, the fibers have an internal structure that holds a stitched conductor firmly without sagging or bunching. Silk also resists humidity and can last many years with little upkeep. While other materials could be tried, the team found that some synthetics lost their shape over time, making the noise-canceling effect uneven.

“Silk gives us a stable platform for these active fibers,” Wei says. “We can wash it by hand, roll it up, and store it, and it still works afterward.” In initial tests, the curtain handled rough treatment well—no frayed conductors or dead spots after several months of daily use.

Outside experts are intrigued. “It’s a neat concept that translates active noise cancellation from headphones to architectural materials,” says Ning Xiang, an acoustics researcher at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute who was not involved in the work. He notes that while the principles are well understood, packaging them into a flimsy sheet that hangs like a normal window curtain is no small feat. “Getting a stable, reliable response from something so thin is tricky,” Xiang says. “A small wrinkle can affect how it vibrates, so the engineering must be careful.”

**Real-World Tests**  
To see how their invention fares outside controlled conditions, Roth’s team arranged a small trial in a Munich apartment that sits beside a commuter rail line. The tenants, who said they’d grown weary of the half-hourly rumble, agreed to replace one conventional cotton drape with the new vibrating silk. The curtain’s controller—about the size of a paperback book—plugged into a standard outlet. Over three weeks, the occupants reported that the harshest train squeals were less piercing, making it easier to watch TV without cranking the volume. Objective measurements suggested an average reduction of about 7 to 9 decibels under typical daily noise, and more during certain frequency ranges. The tenants didn’t call it transformative, but they said it made the living room more tolerable.

“This isn’t going to mute a jackhammer or silence a fire engine siren,” Roth acknowledges. “But when we’re dealing with persistent, medium-level noise—like steady traffic—the curtain can take the sharpness off. You might not notice it as a dramatic drop, more like that background roar is just less grating on your nerves.”

**A Matter of Electricity and Economics**  
One trade-off: the curtain requires a trickle of electricity. The consumption is modest—about the same as leaving a small LED night-light on—but it’s still an ongoing draw, something prospective users must consider. Another challenge is scale. Right now, these fibers must be painstakingly sewn into silk by hand or with a custom loom. Roth says her team is collaborating with a British textile mill to automate the process. Reducing the cost is essential if this technology is ever to move beyond a specialty product.

Cost aside, not everyone wants a wired curtain. “It’s a clever idea, but if I have to plug my window drapes into a wall socket, that might not feel very homey,” says Tony Chon, a researcher at the Fraunhofer Institute for Building Physics in Germany. Chon’s lab investigates building materials that can passively reduce noise. He praises the Manchester team’s approach but suspects that some homeowners may resist “active” curtains, at least initially.

Still, Chon says he can imagine a market. Urban dwellers often struggle with partial sleep due to passing cars or late-night revelers. A light, flexible sound-damping system could let renters improve conditions without drilling holes in the wall or replacing entire window units. It might also help in office settings where open-floor plans amplify chatter. Roth adds that in principle, the curtain’s fibers could be tuned to particular frequencies, targeting, for instance, the low rumble of distant freeway traffic or the high-pitched whine of a leaf blower.

**Next Steps and Future Tinkering**  
Roth’s group is now experimenting with variants. They’re trying thinner conductive yarns, looking for cheaper alternatives to silk, and testing new signal-processing software that can adapt more quickly to changing noise patterns. They’ve also considered incorporating motion sensors so the curtain could “sleep” when a room is empty, saving energy. The curtain might even come in different textures and colors to match interior designs without sacrificing acoustic performance.

“There’s a lot we still don’t know,” Roth says. “This is an early prototype, not a finished product. But we’re seeing that this idea can work in practice, not just in theory.” For the moment, the vibrating silk curtain remains a curious prototype—one that suggests everyday home furnishings may someday do much more than hang quietly, letting the racket roll right in.
title: A Vibrating Curtain of Silk Can Stifle Noise Pollution

text:
A steady stream of cold-stunned sea turtles is arriving at rescue centers in Massachusetts this fall, marking one of the largest waves of hypothermic reptile strandings recorded in Cape Cod in recent years. Volunteers from the New England Aquarium, Mass Audubon’s Wellfleet Bay Wildlife Sanctuary, and other local organizations have been working around the clock to stabilize and treat these weakened animals, many of which appear on beaches, barely moving, as water temperatures plummet.

Cape Cod Bay is a known trap for migratory sea turtles—chiefly Kemp’s ridley, green, and loggerhead turtles—who follow warm currents northward each summer. In milder autumns, they often exit the bay before the mercury drops. But as ocean conditions shift, more turtles linger later into the season, setting the stage for what wildlife responders call “cold-stunning,” a physiological response similar to hypothermia. The turtles lose their ability to swim or feed, drifting ashore in alarming numbers.

“This year we’ve seen hundreds of turtles arriving in need of urgent medical care,” says Dr. Charles Innis, director of animal health at the New England Aquarium. “They come in lethargic, with body temperatures far below normal, often suffering from pneumonia, dehydration, and other complications that can become life-threatening if not addressed promptly.”

On Cape Cod beaches, volunteers routinely patrol the shoreline—especially around high tide—looking for stranded turtles. When they spot one, they wrap it gently in towels and deliver it to the aquarium’s Quincy rehabilitation facility, where staff members gradually warm the reptile and administer fluids, antibiotics, and other treatments. This careful, days-long process helps turtles recover slowly without shocking their systems.

“It’s not as simple as just heating them up,” explains Karen Dourdeville, a sea turtle rescue coordinator at Mass Audubon’s Wellfleet Bay Wildlife Sanctuary. “We raise their body temperature no more than a few degrees a day. If you warm them too quickly, they can go into shock.”

Kemp’s ridley turtles, considered critically endangered, are among the most commonly found species in these strandings. Just decades ago, their numbers were dangerously low. Conservation efforts helped their population begin to rebound, but these cold-stun events are a new source of concern. Green turtles and loggerheads have also been washing ashore in greater numbers than expected.

Scientists point to warming ocean temperatures and shifting prey distributions as factors luring turtles farther north for longer periods. The late return journey puts them at risk when abrupt cold fronts sweep in. “Climate change is certainly playing a role,” says Dr. Kara Dodge, a research scientist at the Anderson Cabot Center for Ocean Life at the New England Aquarium. “These animals are adapted to warm conditions. When the temperature drops quickly, they’re caught off guard.”

The scale of this year’s influx has stretched resources thin. Many of the turtles brought in are no bigger than a dinner plate, though some juveniles approach 50 pounds. Each requires careful medical evaluation. Those that survive receive months of care before staff arrange for their release in warmer southern waters once winter passes.

“I’ve worked marine rescue for over a decade, and I’ve never seen turtle strandings escalate to this degree,” says volunteer rescuer Linda Fisher of Orleans, Massachusetts. “We all love these creatures, and it’s heartbreaking to see them in this state. But I’m hopeful that with intensive rehabilitation, many will make it back into the ocean.”

As global temperatures continue to shift, experts worry that cold-stunning will become more common. For now, however, each fully recovered turtle represents a small but meaningful victory. After months of care, watching a turtle return to the surf—where it belongs—is a reminder that, with dedicated effort and vigilant monitoring, it’s possible to help these vulnerable travelers find their way home.
title: Hundreds of Sea Turtles With Hypothermia Are Washing Up in Cape Cod, Cold-Stunned as Temperatures Drop

A bale of hay might look traditional enough, but on a ranch near Camarillo, California, a few Angus steers have been munching something extra in their daily feed: dried seaweed pellets. The unlikely ingredient isn’t a culinary stunt; it’s part of a serious effort to clean up the beef industry’s image—literally. According to a new study led by researchers at the University of California, Davis, adding small amounts of a certain red seaweed to grazing cattle’s diet cut their methane emissions by nearly 40 percent.

For years, scientists have been trying to find ways to reduce livestock-generated methane, a potent greenhouse gas that traps far more heat per unit than carbon dioxide. Although methane doesn’t linger as long in the atmosphere, it packs an outsized punch in the short term, and cattle are notorious for producing it in their rumen as they digest feed. Many proposed fixes have fallen flat, but feeding seaweed—specifically Asparagopsis taxiformis—appears to tamp down certain microbes in a cow’s gut, thus lowering methane belches without harming the animal’s appetite or growth.

“These results surprised us because we tested the additive in a realistic grazing setting, not just in feedlots,” says Ermias Kebreab, an animal scientist at UC Davis and one of the study’s authors. “We had good indications from controlled trials, but we didn’t know how well it would work when cattle roamed on pastureland.” Previous experiments in confined environments showed even larger methane reductions, sometimes more than 50 or 60 percent. Grazing conditions present a tougher challenge, since cows wander and forage at will. Yet the new field trial still recorded an impressive drop in emissions—roughly 30 to 40 percent—over several months.

To apply the treatment, technicians ground the seaweed into powder and compressed it into pellets that could be easily mixed with molasses and other supplements. The cows didn’t seem to mind the taste. In fact, the animals gained weight at rates similar to their herdmates that didn’t eat seaweed, suggesting no loss of feed efficiency. “We were particularly encouraged that animal health and productivity remained steady,” says Breanna Roque, a ruminant nutrition researcher at UC Davis who helped conduct the feeding trials. “We didn’t want a situation where we fixed one problem but caused another, like reduced growth or lower-quality meat.”

Ranchers who followed the study closely say it’s a welcome development, though they remain cautious about scaling it up. Demand for beef is as strong as ever, and producers are under pressure to shrink their environmental footprint. “We’re always told to cut back greenhouse gases, but it’s tough to do without concrete solutions,” says Austin Ramirez, who manages a family-run ranch in the Central Valley. “If seaweed pellets give us a practical tool, that’s worth exploring. Of course, we’ll have to see if the supply chain can handle it and what it costs.”

Cost is no small matter. While researchers didn’t release detailed pricing, growing and harvesting enough Asparagopsis on a commercial scale could prove a bottleneck. The red seaweed thrives in warm, tropical waters, and most of the current supply comes from pilot farms experimenting with cultivation. Still, a handful of companies have sprung up recently, betting that ranchers—and, indirectly, consumers—will pay a slight premium for more climate-friendly beef.

The environmental benefits could be significant. Methane from livestock is a major contributor to agricultural emissions, and curbing it would help countries meet their climate goals. Although cutting methane alone can’t solve global warming, it can buy time, experts argue. “Reducing livestock methane offers a relatively quick win,” says Frank Mitloehner, an air quality specialist at UC Davis who was not involved in this particular study but has researched greenhouse gases for decades. “If we can cut that emission source even by a modest percentage, the climate math gets a little easier in the near term.”

There are questions beyond economics and supply. For instance, how will consumers feel about cows eating seaweed? Surveys suggest that many people wouldn’t mind, as long as it doesn’t alter the flavor or safety of the beef. Preliminary taste tests show no detectable differences, and the FDA has taken a generally positive stance toward such feed additives, though more research might be required before any official green light. That said, the ranching industry can be slow to adopt new methods. Some producers wonder if dried seaweed pellets will be practical in remote pastures or if weather conditions might pose storage challenges.

The study’s authors acknowledge these hurdles. “It’s early days,” Roque says. “We’re encouraged by the data, but we know wide adoption means working out logistics and showing ranchers that it’s worth their while.” Additional long-term trials are planned to monitor animal health, productivity, and the subtle complexities of managing seaweed diets at scale.

For now, the findings show that a modest sprinkle of seaweed can shift the environmental balance in the cattle industry’s favor. The scientists behind the research stress that it won’t solve climate change on its own, but the next time you see cattle grazing quietly on rolling hills, it’s possible a few are sampling seaweed-laced pellets—an underappreciated twist in the quest to reduce agriculture’s carbon hoofprint.
title: Eating Seaweed Could Make Cows Less Gassy, Slashing Methane Emissions From Grazing by Nearly 40 Percent

text:
Before the English Restoration, audiences in London’s playhouses might see kings, fools, gods, or devils, but never an actual woman earning her living on the public stage. Men and boys took every role, fashioning elaborate costumes and falsettos to portray queens, young maidens, and even nuns. This convention held for generations—until December 8, 1660, when a woman stepped forward under the stage lights, performed for a paying crowd, and changed English theater’s course. Even now, more than 360 years later, we cannot say with absolute certainty who she was.

Many scholars argue the actress was Margaret Hughes, who is recorded as having played Desdemona in a production of **Othello** staged by the King’s Company at the Vere Street Theatre. Others suggest it might have been Anne Marshall or a different performer whose name has slipped into obscurity. Regardless, this mysterious debutant has become a legendary figure, ushering in a new era of professional female performers—a development unimaginable during the strictly all-male traditions of Elizabethan and Jacobean drama.

Dr. Clare McManus, an early modern theater historian at the University of Roehampton, reflects on the uncertainty. “We know a play was performed, we know it included a woman in a female role for the first time on the English public stage, and we know that many eyewitnesses were stunned,” she says. “The problem is the historical record doesn’t always give us a tidy name. This fog of ambiguity leaves room for debate—and that debate has persisted since the 17th century.”

In his diary, Samuel Pepys never quite pinned down this actress’s identity, though he did remark on seeing women perform around that time. Other observers wrote of their surprise and delight, marveling at the novelty of seeing a genuine woman’s face where, just months earlier, only painted boys had stood. Charles II’s court had recently reestablished the monarchy, and the king’s fascination with Continental styles of theater—where women had already been performing—likely played a role in encouraging this shift.

Before long, the presence of female performers no longer shocked playgoers. Actresses such as Nell Gwyn, Elizabeth Barry, and Anne Bracegirdle became major attractions in London’s bustling theaters. Yet, McManus notes that this initial breakthrough moment is still overshadowed by the namelessness of its principal pioneer. “It’s ironic that the actress who opened the door remains a shadowy figure,” she says. “We celebrate this watershed day, but we’re forced to rely on fragments of evidence. In truth, no single playbill or letter clearly states her identity.”

Contemporary writers often described the first professional English actress as daring simply for appearing in public—a striking shift in an era when women’s voices and bodies had been policed and restricted. Soon after 1660, audiences grew accustomed to seeing actresses in tragic roles, witty heroines, and even breeches parts (women dressed as men). Ticket sales soared. Playwrights adapted their scripts to better suit female performers, introducing complex female characters who could be convincingly portrayed by women rather than by teenage boys.

Over time, the anonymous figure behind that first public performance became both a symbol of freedom and a riddle historians continue to puzzle over. We have signatures on later contracts, memoirs that mention famous actresses, paintings that depict 17th-century stage luminaries—but the exact name of the woman who broke that barrier on a December evening in 1660 refuses to come into clear focus.

“The original records were never meant to serve as a neat origin story,” McManus observes. “They were day-to-day notes and casual remarks. People were excited, but not always careful in giving us the details we crave now.”

So we remember the event itself: one performance, one woman standing where no English woman had publicly stood before. She altered the sound, sight, and spirit of the stage. While we might never assign her the certainty of a name, the moment she claimed a spot under the stage’s glare still resonates every time an actress steps into the spotlight.
title: A Woman Appeared on the English Stage for the First Time on This Day in 1660, Transforming the World of Theater Forever

text:
In a scrubby patch of rainforest in central Panama, a small brown frog with bright speckles has begun doing something biologists weren’t sure they’d ever see again: surviving in numbers. Several years back, nearly every amphibian here seemed doomed. A deadly fungal pathogen called **Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis**, or Bd for short, had slashed local frog populations by as much as 90 percent. Species that were once abundant along streamsides and leaf-strewn trails vanished almost overnight. Now, despite ongoing infections, a handful of survivors are croaking and courting again. The mere sight of them gives researchers reason to believe that certain frogs can evolve resistance—or at least tolerance—to a fungus long feared to be unstoppable.

**A Global Killer on the Move**  
Bd emerged as a global threat in the late 20th century, ravaging amphibians on nearly every continent except Antarctica. By the early 2000s, the fungus had contributed to declines or extinctions of over 500 species, making it one of the most destructive pathogens documented in wildlife. It reproduces in a frog’s skin, interfering with fluid balance and leading to cardiac arrest. It doesn’t help that frogs absorb water and salts directly through their skin, so the fungus essentially wrecks their most vital interface with the environment. For many years, scientists struggled to find any bright spots amid the carnage.

“There were a few holdouts, but the story was grim,” says Dr. Karen Lips, a biologist at the University of Maryland who witnessed the fungus’s devastating impact in Panama. “We’d arrive at streams we knew were full of frogs just a year before, and find almost nothing left alive.” She and her colleagues suspected that if any amphibians were to persist, they’d have to adapt quickly—either physiologically or through changes in behavior or skin chemistry.

**Signs of Resistance and Resilience**  
Recent evidence suggests some frogs are indeed fighting back. Researchers led by Dr. Jamie Voyles, an ecologist at the University of Nevada, Reno, have shown that certain populations, once hard hit, are stabilizing or even rebounding. The survivors aren’t merely lucky individuals who avoided infection; instead, some frogs can now carry Bd on their skin without succumbing. In one study published in *Science*, Voyles and her team identified changes in the frogs’ immune responses, including more potent antimicrobial peptides—tiny molecules in their skin that zap pathogens.

“There’s a shift in how these frogs’ immune systems function,” says Voyles. “We’re seeing differences in the composition of their skin microbiome, too—beneficial bacteria that might help fend off the fungus.” These alterations aren’t dramatic superpowers. They’re subtle changes spread across populations, but they could mean the difference between extinction and survival.

It’s not just about skin defenses. Some frogs may now regulate their body temperatures more strategically. Others might choose microhabitats that are less conducive to the fungus’s growth. The result is that at least a few species are coexisting with Bd rather than being obliterated by it. “We’ve gone from disaster mode—‘All these amphibians are doomed’—to recognizing that nature sometimes comes up with remarkable solutions,” Lips says.

**New Tools to Tip the Balance**  
Even with these glimmers of hope, frogs can use some help. Some scientists are testing approaches to give amphibians a leg up. One idea is to seed frog habitats with beneficial microbes—bacteria that can slow the fungus’s spread. Another involves carefully targeted antifungal treatments in certain breeding areas. In places like Panama and Costa Rica, researchers have also tried reintroducing captive-bred frogs, hoping that controlled conditions might allow them to mature with stronger defenses before facing Bd in the wild.

Zoos and labs are refining treatments like “probiotic baths,” which involve soaking frogs in water teeming with protective microbes. “It’s not a silver bullet,” says Dr. Luke Linhoff, a wildlife veterinarian with the Panama Amphibian Rescue and Conservation Project. “But if we can boost their natural defenses, we may give them that extra margin they need.” He notes that even minor improvements in survival odds can help species struggling to gain a foothold after catastrophic declines.

In addition, some teams are using genetic tools to understand precisely which genes change when frogs become more tolerant. By decoding these pathways, scientists hope to identify markers of resistance that could guide conservation strategies. If they know which populations carry these promising traits, they can prioritize habitats and shield them from logging or pollution. None of these interventions guarantee success, but they offer options beyond watchful despair.

**Adjusting to a New Normal**  
Today, Bd remains a massive threat. Many amphibian species haven’t yet shown signs of bouncing back. Some that were common are functionally extinct in the wild. Others persist only in carefully guarded breeding centers. Still, the evolving defenses of certain frogs provide a blueprint for what recovery might look like. It won’t be a simple return to the past: the amphibian communities of tomorrow may be different in composition and behavior, and researchers must accept a certain amount of trial-and-error in their interventions.

Despite the uncertainties, Lips is encouraged by what she’s seen in recent field seasons. “When we first came face-to-face with this fungus, it seemed insurmountable,” she says. “But we’re finally seeing frogs that have learned to live alongside it.” Around the rainforest streams and mossy boulders where Bd first announced itself so catastrophically, at least a few amphibians are forging a future—even if that future looks unlike anything we’ve known before.

text:
For decades, a tiny, skin-infecting fungus known as Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd) has caused catastrophic declines in frog populations worldwide. Regions of Central and South America have borne the brunt, but similar devastation has occurred everywhere from Australia’s Wet Tropics to the Sierra Nevada in California. Species after species fell victim to chytridiomycosis, the lethal disease triggered by Bd. In some places, entire choruses of nighttime callers disappeared.

Now, in certain streams where frogs had nearly vanished, scientists are hearing something unexpected: the familiar croaks and chirps of new generations. Researchers have identified a handful of frog species showing signs of mounting resistance to the fungus. This shift—though still modest—is offering new hope that amphibians are not as defenseless as once believed.

“It’s not a simple comeback story,” says Dr. Karen Lips, an amphibian biologist at the University of Maryland who has studied frog declines for more than 20 years. “We’re not seeing massive rebounds across the board, but we are seeing species that were hit hard now surviving in the presence of Bd. They don’t always thrive as they did before, but they persist.”

One line of evidence comes from field observations in Panama, where the fungus raced through frog communities in the early 2000s. Many species, including the once-common harlequin frogs, went from abundant to scarce in a matter of seasons. But in recent years, researchers have spotted survivors and their offspring clinging on in small but stable populations. According to Dr. Jamie Voyles, a disease ecologist at the University of Nevada, Reno, certain frog species appear to be adapting at the immunological level. “We’ve identified subtle changes in their skin peptides and beneficial skin microbes that may be helping them cope,” she says. “These defenses don’t wipe out the fungus, but they seem to keep it in check.”

The frog’s skin is more than just a barrier—it’s an entire ecosystem. Microbes living on the surface can influence how well Bd takes hold. Some bacteria release antifungal compounds that hinder the pathogen. In places where frogs are rebounding, scientists have found higher proportions of protective microbes. That’s led to experiments in which frogs are treated with probiotic “cocktails” to bolster their skin’s natural defenses. While these attempts are still at an early stage, preliminary results suggest the microbiome approach could complement other conservation tactics.

Another strategy under consideration involves selective breeding. If scientists can identify certain genetic variants that confer resistance, they might create lineages of frogs better equipped to survive with Bd in the wild. But Dr. Lips cautions that these interventions have to be done carefully. “We’re talking about complex ecosystems, not just frogs in isolation,” she says. “If we release a frog population that hasn’t interacted with its native parasites, predators, or competitors for years, we could disrupt the local balance. We have to think holistically.”

In parallel, some researchers are testing targeted antifungals in controlled environments. Amphibians are collected from disease hotspots, treated in laboratories or field stations, then re-released. This is no small feat. “Handling wild frogs repeatedly is stressful to them—and us,” says Dr. Roberto Ibáñez, a scientific coordinator at the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute in Panama, who has been involved in some of these projects. “Still, without trying these approaches, we can’t learn what works.”

The global scale of Bd’s impact means that solutions won’t be one-size-fits-all. The fungus thrives in cool, moist conditions—hence its success in mountain cloud forests—and different frog species have different vulnerabilities. Some species, like the mountain yellow-legged frog in California, have shown that, over time, populations can develop higher survival rates even in infected habitats. Others remain perilously close to extinction.

At the same time, there’s mounting interest in understanding why some regions have been less affected. For instance, in certain parts of Asia where Bd is present, it hasn’t caused widespread die-offs. Studying these “tolerance hotspots” could provide clues. Scientists wonder if local amphibians have coexisted with the fungus for so long that a stable equilibrium developed.

Underlying all these efforts is the realization that amphibian declines—once widely viewed as unstoppable—may at least be mitigated. “A decade ago, I would’ve told you that Bd was an absolute death sentence for many species,” says Dr. Voyles. “Now, we’re seeing that some populations are evolving. It’s slow, it’s partial, but it’s real.”

Conservation groups, including the Panama Amphibian Rescue and Conservation Project and the Amphibian Survival Alliance, are banking on these findings to inform their next moves. They’ve begun to tailor their interventions based on local species’ responses, whether that means focusing on genetic screening, tweaking probiotic formulations, or coordinating habitat restoration to improve frogs’ baseline health. Healthy frogs, after all, are better positioned to resist infection.

No one is declaring victory. The world’s amphibians still face habitat loss, pollution, climate change, and invasive predators. But Bd, once seemingly an unbeatable enemy, may not remain unchallenged forever. “What’s unfolding now,” says Dr. Lips, “is a kind of evolutionary arms race. The fungus doesn’t vanish, but neither do the frogs. They’re finding ways to coexist, and that’s something we couldn’t have imagined 20 years ago.”

For conservationists, even modest signs of resistance are cause for cautious optimism. Amid the relentless tide of wildlife declines, the idea that frogs can learn new survival tricks suggests that with the right help, nature can adapt. It’s a tough lesson—earned through painstaking fieldwork and countless hours of lab experiments—but it points toward a future where frogs and fungus share the forest floor without one side disappearing entirely.
title: How Frogs Are Kicking Back Against a Lethal Fungus

text:
Alligators uprooted by Hurricane Milton are emerging in neighborhoods far from their usual habitats, and wildlife officials say homeowners should steer clear of the animals, even if they seem sluggish or cornered. Reports have surfaced across multiple Florida counties, with some residents stumbling upon alligators in their driveways, near their birdfeeders, or even lurking behind loading docks at suburban shopping centers.

The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission estimates that at least a few hundred alligators have ventured beyond their typical marshy homes since Milton’s intense storm surge pushed water inland late last week. While these reptiles are not generally aggressive unless threatened, officials say people need to keep their distance. “They may look slow on dry ground, but they can bolt forward or whip their tails in a split second,” said Dana Lowe, a biologist with the commission. “We’re advising everyone not to try shooing them away or poking them with sticks.”

The sudden appearance of alligators in unexpected spots can be startling. At a residential block in Lake County, an eight-foot gator surprised a family returning from the grocery store. Melissa Ortiz, who lives two houses down, recounted her neighbor’s experience: “They got home at dusk, turned on the headlights, and there it was, right by the mailbox. Nobody could believe it.” Eventually, wildlife officers arrived and carefully coaxed the reptile back toward a nearby canal, where water levels had finally started to recede.

Local wildlife trappers are busier than usual. Some are fielding calls at twice their normal rate, and the backlog has led to impatient residents taking matters into their own hands—something officials strongly discourage. “We’ve had a few folks try to rope an alligator themselves or lure it away with a plate of raw chicken,” said Mark Heinz, a longtime trapper based in Orlando. “That’s dangerous. You can’t predict how these animals will respond under stress.”

Even unexpected resources have popped up to handle the surge. A few veterinary clinics that typically treat domestic pets have been asked by authorities to store sedatives or offer their spare kennels to wildlife officers who need holding areas for displaced gators. So far, no serious injuries have been reported, but local authorities emphasize that it’s only a matter of time before someone tests their luck.

David Fuller, a wildlife rehabilitator in Volusia County, said the sudden displacement of alligators shows how deeply inland flooding can affect ecosystems. “When rivers overflow and marshes blend into suburban streets, wild animals just follow the water,” he said. “These gators haven’t chosen to be out there—Milton’s surge put them in this position.”

For now, the official guidance remains simple: stay indoors if you see an alligator on your property, call local authorities, and wait it out. Ortiz, the Lake County resident, learned that lesson quickly. “We had one right at the end of the block last night,” she said. “We stayed inside until the wildlife folks came. Better that than getting too close.”
title: Alligators Displaced by Milton Are Turning Up in Unexpected Places

text:
When an image popped up on a Reddit thread dedicated to obscure pop-culture sightings, most users scrolled right past. It showed a dimly lit backstage corridor, six people standing shoulder-to-shoulder. The first five were easily recognizable names—movie stars, a television host, a chart-topping singer, a stand-up comedian, and a retired basketball legend. The sixth person, lurking a step behind the others, wore a baseball cap, glasses, and a guarded half-smile. Labelled only as “celebrity number six,” that individual’s identity became the subject of an unexpectedly intense online hunt.

This collective effort, which started on a Tuesday evening in early September and lasted nearly a month, pulled in thousands of participants from Twitter, TikTok, and multiple private Discord servers. Some people ran image searches through digitized yearbooks, while others flipped through scanned copies of entertainment magazines from the early ’90s. A few enlisted help from autograph collectors who specialize in Hollywood’s lesser-known figures. Others reached out directly to production staff of old variety specials, since the photo’s original source was rumored to be a behind-the-scenes snapshot from a forgotten TV benefit aired on a local Los Angeles station decades ago.

“At first, I joined in just because I had ten spare minutes,” said Nina Coleman, a 32-year-old set decorator in Atlanta who posted side-by-side facial comparisons of potential matches. “Then I got hooked. The more I dug, the more I realized how much I rely on other people’s expertise. One person would identify the hallway as belonging to a certain studio, someone else would recall that studio was used for a 1993 charity telethon, and next thing you know, we had a solid lead.”

Participants who spend their weekends identifying obscure band members in music videos or comparing still frames from old VHS recordings have done this sort of thing before, but rarely with such a varied team. The crowd included a New York-based casting assistant, a Chicago archivist who specializes in early cable broadcasts, and a group of Los Angeles film students with a knack for freeze-framing out-of-print documentaries. The search gradually took on the feel of a community project, with volunteers maintaining a shared spreadsheet that listed every guess—more than 400 names at one point—and noted why each was ruled out.

“All these tactics illustrate the power of crowdsourcing,” said David Sternberg, a media historian at UCLA who followed the effort from the sidelines. “When you get enough people contributing their niche knowledge, you fill in gaps that any single researcher would struggle to cover. It’s a form of puzzle-solving that’s unique to our digital age. You can have a hobbyist in Kansas matching a wallpaper pattern to a known green room, and a Hollywood lighting technician confirming the era based on the type of Fresnel lamps visible in the background.”

The turning point came when a user who goes by “MaraKnows” recalled seeing a similar event while cataloging old press photos for a private collector. They remembered a minor television actor who frequently appeared at charity events but never scored major film roles. That memory prompted a flurry of posts, and after more cross-checking with talent rosters from a 1993 earthquake relief broadcast, one name kept resurfacing: Gary Thurman, a stand-in and occasional warm-up comic who worked behind the scenes on numerous Los Angeles-based productions.

Initially, nobody could find official credits for Thurman beyond a few fleeting mentions in trade publications. Eventually, a longtime union publicist stepped in. The publicist confirmed that Thurman had indeed volunteered at an event in Burbank in early 1994. A staff photo from that event, found in a digital archive hosted by the Los Angeles Public Library, matched the posture, cap, and glasses of the mystery figure. After careful verification, the community concluded that “celebrity number six” was actually just a well-liked bit player in Hollywood’s busy ecosystem—someone known mainly to crew members and local comics, not the household name many expected.

Reactions ranged from amused disappointment to genuine satisfaction. “I’d never heard of Gary Thurman before,” said DeAndre Miller, a documentary editor who hopped into the search after seeing a TikTok snippet about it. “But I guess that’s the point. Sometimes, the solution isn’t a huge star. Sometimes it’s a guy who quietly helped make other people look good.”

As users updated the Reddit thread’s title to reflect the discovery, most agreed that the process, rather than the outcome, was what really mattered. “We showed that no single database or recognition app can beat a crowd of curious humans,” said Coleman. “It took a whole bunch of us, comparing notes, making odd guesses, checking obscure sources. Honestly, that’s the best part.”
title: It Took an Army of Internet Sleuths to Find ‘Celebrity Number Six’

text:
Tossing a few capital letters into an email might seem trivial, but try telling that to a generation raised on text messages, TikTok captions, and Slack threads that never bother with the shift key. Now that these individuals are moving deeper into the workforce, some are feeling a new kind of pressure: the expectation that they present themselves in writing as adults—capital letters and all.

At a mid-sized marketing agency in Minneapolis, brand strategist Amanda Farrell recalls a tense moment last December when a new hire’s email arrived looking more like a casual group text than a professional note. “He wrote: ‘hey team, gonna run these numbers by tom. b right back.’ I didn’t know whether to laugh or panic,” she says. Her manager hinted that such informality wasn’t a big deal for Slack or text messages among peers, but that email should reflect “grownup” formatting. Farrell says the new hire got the message. The next morning he replied with a follow-up: “Hey Team, I’ll be sending the updated metrics shortly.” She almost imagined him wincing as he typed the capital “H” in “Hey.”

Plenty of veterans in corporate offices have seen email styles evolve over the decades. Early internet correspondences bristled with ALL CAPS subject lines and chaotic punctuation. Then came a period of pristine professionalism—subject lines carefully cased, salutations and sign-offs neatly aligned. Younger workers influenced by social media norms often find the shift key optional, assuming that as long as the content is clear, nobody cares about capitalization.

But many people do. “Workplace communication is a dance we’re all still learning, and typography is a step in that dance,” says Susan Brenner, a communications professor at Northwestern University’s School of Communication. Brenner studies how nonverbal cues translate into digital text formats. “Capitalization signals formality, respect, and a willingness to play by longstanding rules,” she says. “This is not a small thing. It’s not an empty ritual. It’s a way to say, ‘I take this interaction seriously.’”

At a tech startup in Austin, Texas, product manager Colin Ray spent his first six months typing everything in lowercase. He admits he simply never formed the habit of using caps beyond the occasional “LOL.” When a senior colleague gently reminded him that investors sometimes get looped in on email chains, he decided to adjust. “It felt weird at first,” Ray says. “I typed like i always do, and then i went back and forced myself to fix the capitalization. After a few weeks, it got easier.” Still, he confesses that if he’s just messaging a close teammate on Slack, he might revert to all lowercase. “It’s like wearing a nice shirt when you’re meeting a client, and a T-shirt when you’re just talking to your buddy who sits next to you,” he says.

Not everyone is ready to give in. There are holdouts who see the insistence on capitalization as fussy. “I think it’s elitist,” says Lucy Tran, a graphic designer in Brooklyn who works remotely for a fashion brand. She rarely capitalizes her first-person pronoun “I,” and her memos bristle with a certain free-flowing style: “hey dmitri, got the new mockups—will push them after lunch.” Her boss hasn’t complained, and Tran sees her lowercase approach as a signature, a subtle stand against conformity. “I don’t think uppercase letters are going to make my ideas better or clearer,” she says. “If the content is good, who cares if i capitalized the first letter of the sentence?”

Some managers feel caught in the middle, not wanting to sound like old-school grammar police while still maintaining some semblance of professionalism. A human resources director at a Philadelphia insurance firm—who asked not to be named because she’s still navigating these norms—says her team had a formal discussion last fall. They concluded that internal Slack messages could remain casual, but external emails and especially client reports should reflect standard writing conventions, including capitalization. “We decided it’s like dressing business-casual in person,” she explains. “No one’s asking you to wear a three-piece suit, but sweatpants are out.”

The pressure to appear “grownup” in writing isn’t just about aesthetics. Some believe that older clients might subconsciously question the competence of a person who can’t manage a capital “I” or the first letter of a brand’s name. “The risk is subtle,” says Tom Davenport, a freelance consultant who advises small businesses on branding. “A CEO reading a pitch deck might not say out loud, ‘This person can’t capitalize their letters, I’m dropping their proposal.’ But tiny signals add up. We all know presentation matters. It’s not just what you say; it’s how you say it—even how you type it.”

A few companies have turned this into a running joke. In May, a media startup in Seattle reportedly created a Slack channel called #caps-training to help interns adjust their writing style before sending emails to advertisers. According to one staffer, participants teased each other, awarding virtual “gold stars” for correctly capitalized sentences. The idea was to remove tension and turn learning a small professional skill into a game. “We had kids fresh out of college who wrote beautifully, but looked like they were texting their roommates,” the staffer says. “A few rounds of good-natured ribbing later, everybody was typing like they’d been doing it forever.”

This subtle shift may never feel entirely natural to some. But, as Brenner at Northwestern points out, language always changes, and so do its norms. “A generation from now, maybe everything is lowercase, and we’ll look back at uppercase letters as this strange relic,” she says. “For now, though, in many offices, using proper capitalization can feel like a low-stakes rite of passage—a small signal that you’ve arrived.”
